plain: A rule that splits blame for a crash by percentage, reducing payouts by your own share of fault.
snappy: A liability rule apportioning damages by each party's percentage of fault rather than barring a partly-at-fault claimant.
detail: Under comparative negligence, if you're found 30% at fault for a crash, you recover 70% of your damages. It softens the old all-or-nothing contributory-negligence rule that barred any recovery for a plaintiff even slightly to blame. States vary: "pure" comparative lets you recover even at 99% fault, while "modified" versions cut you off at 50% or 51%. Adjusters and courts haggle over these percentages in nearly every disputed auto claim.

plain: Money a court awards to put an injured person back where they were — medical bills, lost wages, pain.
snappy: Damages intended to reimburse a plaintiff for actual losses, both economic (bills, lost income) and non-economic (pain, suffering).
detail: Compensatory damages are the make-whole part of a liability award: they reimburse what the harm actually cost. Economic damages cover the countable losses — medical bills, lost wages, repair costs — while non-economic damages put a number on pain, suffering, and lost enjoyment of life. They're what a liability policy is built to pay, distinct from punitive damages meant to punish. Sizing them is the core of every settlement negotiation and jury verdict.

plain: Business coverage for harm caused by work you already finished — like a deck that collapses months after you built it.
snappy: The general liability coverage for bodily injury or property damage arising from a contractor's work after it is finished and handed over.
detail: Completed operations covers the long tail of a contractor's risk: the wiring that sparks a fire a year after the job, the deck that gives way once you've left the site. Because the harm surfaces after the work is done, claims can arrive long after the project closed, so this part of a general liability policy is where occurrence-based coverage earns its keep. Tradespeople watch it closely, since dropping the policy can leave finished jobs unprotected.

plain: Car insurance for damage that isn't a crash — theft, fire, hail, vandalism, or hitting a deer.
snappy: First-party coverage paying for non-collision losses to the covered vehicle: theft, fire, weather, vandalism, animal strikes.
detail: Comprehensive coverage — sometimes called "other than collision" — handles the things that happen to a parked or driving car short of a crash: theft, a cracked windshield, hail, flood, fire, vandalism, or a deer in the road. It carries its own deductible and, like collision coverage, is required by lenders. Together the two make up "full coverage." In hail- and flood-prone regions, comprehensive claims drive much of the premium.

plain: Staying silent about a fact you knew the insurer needed — which can void the policy later.
snappy: An applicant's failure to disclose a material fact the insurer would need to assess the risk, potentially voiding coverage.
detail: Concealment is the sin of omission in insurance: not an outright lie, but staying quiet about something material the insurer should have known — a prior loss, a health condition, a side business run from the home. Because insurance rests on utmost good faith, deliberate concealment of a material fact can let the insurer rescind the policy or deny a claim. It sits beside material misrepresentation, which is telling the insurer something untrue rather than withholding the truth.

plain: When two causes — one covered, one excluded — combine to produce a loss, raising the question of whether to pay.
snappy: A situation where a covered peril and an excluded peril together cause a loss, complicating whether coverage applies.
detail: Concurrent causation is a coverage headache: a loss results from two perils acting together, one covered and one excluded — wind-driven rain plus flood, say. Which one controls? Courts have split, some asking which peril was the efficient proximate cause, others enforcing policy wording strictly. Insurers responded with anti-concurrent-causation clauses that deny the whole loss if an excluded peril contributed at all. It's why a hurricane claim can turn on the fine distinction between wind damage and flood damage.

plain: A document giving you temporary life-insurance coverage while the insurer finishes reviewing your application.
snappy: A receipt providing interim life or health coverage from the application date, conditional on the applicant proving insurable.
detail: When you apply for life insurance and pay the first premium, a conditional receipt can start coverage right away — but only conditionally. If you'd have qualified under the insurer's rules and then die before the policy issues, the claim is paid; if you wouldn't have qualified, coverage never truly began. It bridges the gap during underwriting, and the fine print on exactly what condition must be met is what decides whether a death in that window is covered.

plain: The fine-print duties you must meet — like reporting a loss promptly — or the insurer can refuse to pay.
snappy: Policy provisions setting out the duties and procedures the insured must follow for coverage to apply.
detail: Notify the insurer promptly, cooperate with the investigation, protect property from further damage, submit a proof of loss on time — these strings are attached to every grant of coverage. Break a material one and the insurer may deny an otherwise valid claim. This section is also where you find how disputes are resolved, how other insurance is coordinated, and the right of the insurer to inspect or audit.

plain: The first two years of a life policy, when the insurer can still investigate and void it for lies on the application.
snappy: An initial period, usually two years, during which an insurer may rescind a policy for misstatements; after it, claims stand.
detail: During the contestability period — typically the first two years — a life insurer can review the application after a death claim and rescind the policy for material misrepresentation, refunding premiums instead of paying. Once it passes, the incontestability clause locks the policy in: even a discovered misstatement can no longer undo it, except for outright fraud in some states. It's why deaths soon after a policy is issued draw extra scrutiny.

plain: The backup who collects the life insurance if your first-choice beneficiary has already died.
snappy: A beneficiary who receives policy proceeds only if every primary beneficiary has died before the insured.
detail: Naming a contingent beneficiary is the safety net: if your primary beneficiary dies before you and you never update the form, the proceeds go to the contingent rather than into your estate, where probate and creditors can reach them. Spouses are often primary, children contingent. Keeping both designations current after deaths, divorces, and births is the single most overlooked piece of life insurance housekeeping.

plain: A bonus an insurer pays an agency for the volume or profitability of the business it brings in.
snappy: Extra producer compensation based on the volume, growth, or loss ratio of the business placed with an insurer, beyond base commission.
detail: On top of base commission, insurers often pay agencies a contingent commission — a year-end bonus geared to how much profitable business they steered to the carrier, measured by volume, growth, or loss ratio. It rewards producers for sending good risks and lots of them. The arrangement drew scrutiny in the mid-2000s when undisclosed contingent deals were found to bias brokers' recommendations against their clients' interests, prompting disclosure rules so buyers can see the incentive behind the advice.

plain: Coverage for liability you take on by signing a contract, not liability the law would have imposed anyway.
snappy: The general liability coverage for liability a policyholder assumes under contract, such as a hold harmless or indemnification clause.
detail: Contractual liability is how a general liability policy responds when you've promised, in a signed agreement, to shoulder another party's exposure. Construction and vendor contracts are full of these assumptions, and without the coverage a hold harmless promise could fall outside the policy. Insurers cover liability assumed under an insured contract — a defined category — while watching for over-broad clauses that pile on risk the underwriter never priced.

plain: A term life policy you can later switch to permanent coverage without a new medical exam.
snappy: A term policy with an option to convert to permanent insurance without re-proving insurability, within a set window.
detail: A convertible term policy carries a valuable option: within a stated period you can convert some or all of it to permanent coverage at standard rates without a new medical exam, even if your health has since collapsed. It protects against becoming uninsurable. Buyers who expect their needs or finances to change later pay a little more for term that converts, locking in future access to permanent insurance.

plain: The rules that decide which plan pays first when you're covered by two of them.
snappy: Rules determining the order in which two or more health plans pay when a person is covered by more than one.
detail: When a child is on both parents' plans, or a worker has employer coverage plus a spouse's, coordination of benefits sets which plan is primary and pays first and which is secondary and picks up the remainder. The goal is to stop double payment while making sure the patient isn't shortchanged. The "birthday rule" — the parent whose birthday falls earlier in the year pays first — is the classic tiebreaker for kids.

plain: A flat fee — say $25 — you hand over at the doctor or pharmacy, with insurance covering the rest.
snappy: A fixed dollar amount the insured pays for a covered health service, separate from the deductible and coinsurance.
detail: A $30 copay for a primary-care visit or $10 for a generic drug is predictable, which is why plans use copays for routine care — you know the cost before you walk in. Copays may or may not count toward your deductible, but they do count toward the out-of-pocket maximum. You'll see them printed on your insurance card next to the network type so the front desk knows what to collect.

plain: Extra help on a marketplace plan that shrinks your deductible and copays if your income is low enough.
snappy: An ACA subsidy that lowers deductibles, copays, and the out-of-pocket maximum for lower-income silver-plan enrollees.
detail: On top of the premium tax credit, a cost-sharing reduction quietly upgrades a silver marketplace plan for lower-income buyers — slashing the deductible, copays, and out-of-pocket maximum so the plan pays a bigger share of each bill. You must pick a silver plan to get it. Many eligible people miss out by choosing bronze for the lower premium, not realising they're leaving this help on the table.

plain: The protection your policy actually provides — the specific losses it promises to pay for.
snappy: The scope of protection a policy grants: which perils, people, and property it pays for, up to stated limits.
detail: Coverage is what you're buying. A homeowners policy might pay for fire and theft but not flood; an auto policy splits protection into liability, collision, and comprehensive. Agents talk about "gaps in coverage" when a real-world loss falls outside every section of the policy. Reading which coverages you have — and at what limit — is the difference between a paid claim and an unpleasant surprise.

plain: The event that determines which policy year, and which insurer, has to respond to a claim.
snappy: The event or condition that activates coverage, deciding which policy period responds to a loss that unfolds over time.
detail: For losses that develop slowly — a leak that rots a structure over years, an illness from long-ago exposure — the coverage trigger decides which policy answers: the one in force when the harm began, when it became apparent, or when the claim was made. Occurrence policies trigger on when the injury happened; claims-made policies trigger on when the claim is filed. Long-tail disputes over asbestos and pollution turned the trigger question into some of insurance's most litigated ground.

plain: How much statistical trust to put in a group's own loss data versus the broader average, given its size.
snappy: An actuarial weighting of how much an individual or group's own experience should influence its rate versus broader data.
detail: Credibility answers a basic pricing question: should this account's own claims history set its price, or is it too small to trust? Actuaries assign a weight between zero and one — full credibility for a large, data-rich group, partial for a small one — blending the account's own experience with the wider class average accordingly. It's the math under experience rating, explaining why a fleet of a thousand trucks is priced largely on its own record while a single car leans on the class.

plain: The regulatory rule deciding when an insurer may count ceded risk as truly off its books — depending on the reinsurer's strength.
snappy: Statutory rules governing when a ceding insurer may reduce its liabilities for risk transferred to a reinsurer, based on the reinsurer's status or collateral.
detail: Reinsurance only relieves a ceding company's regulatory burden if the rules let it take credit for it: the insurer may reduce its statutory liabilities by the ceded amount, but only when the reinsurer is authorized in the state or posts collateral to secure the obligation. The requirements are toughest for offshore and unauthorized reinsurers, protecting against worthless reinsurance recoverables. The rules, modernized through the NAIC and international agreements, are what make reinsurance count toward solvency rather than just being a private side bet.

plain: A score from your credit history that many insurers use to help set your premium.
snappy: A score derived from credit data that insurers use, where allowed, as a predictor of future claims and pricing.
detail: Insurers in most states use a credit-based insurance score — built from your credit history but distinct from a lending credit score — because it statistically predicts claims. Better credit often means a lower premium, a practice critics call unfair to lower-income drivers and that a few states (California, Hawaii, Massachusetts) ban for auto. It's a quiet but powerful factor that surprises drivers who don't realise credit affects their car insurance.

plain: A policy that pays a lump sum of cash if you're diagnosed with a serious illness like cancer or a heart attack.
snappy: Supplemental coverage paying a fixed cash benefit on diagnosis of a covered serious illness, used however the insured wishes.
detail: Critical illness insurance pays a tax-free lump sum — say $20,000 — on diagnosis of a covered condition such as cancer, heart attack, or stroke, no matter your medical bills. The cash can cover the deductible, lost income, or travel for treatment. Sold as a cheap voluntary benefit at work, it plugs gaps a high-deductible health plan leaves. Critics note the narrow list of covered conditions and the fine print on what counts.

plain: A clause letting a policyholder collect directly from the reinsurer if the primary insurer goes broke.
snappy: A provision allowing a policyholder or beneficiary to claim directly against the reinsurer if the ceding insurer becomes insolvent.
detail: Normally reinsurance is a private matter between insurers, with no link to the policyholder. A cut-through endorsement pierces that wall: if the primary insurer fails, the named insured can collect the reinsured portion straight from the reinsurer. Lenders and large commercial insureds sometimes demand one when buying coverage from a small or shaky carrier backed by a strong reinsurer, so an insolvency upstream doesn't leave their claim unpaid.

plain: Coverage for the costs of a data breach or cyberattack — from notifying customers to paying ransom and lawsuits.
snappy: Coverage for losses from data breaches and cyber incidents, including response costs, liability to affected parties, and business interruption.
detail: Cyber liability insurance answers the modern breach: it funds forensic investigation, customer notification, credit monitoring, regulatory fines, lawsuits from exposed individuals, and increasingly the ransom and downtime of an attack. Standard property and general liability policies were never built for digital harm, so this stand-alone line filled the gap and grew fast. Underwriters now demand real security controls — multi-factor login, backups, employee training — before they'll quote, making the coverage a lever for better security.

plain: The money a life insurance policy pays out when the insured person dies.
snappy: The sum a life insurer pays beneficiaries when the insured dies, generally free of federal income tax.
detail: The death benefit is the whole point of life insurance — the face amount paid to beneficiaries when the insured dies, usually income-tax-free. On permanent policies it can be the face amount alone or the face amount plus accumulated cash value, depending on the option chosen. Riders like accelerated death benefit let a terminally ill insured tap part of it early. Annuities also carry a death benefit for money left at death.

plain: The front page of your policy listing who's covered, for what, and for how much.
snappy: The summary page of the policy stating the named insured, coverages, limits, deductibles, premium, and policy period.
detail: The declarations page — "the dec page" — is the cheat sheet agents pull up first. It personalises the standard policy form with your name, address, vehicle or building, the coverages you bought, their limits and deductibles, and the premium. A lender asking for "proof of insurance" usually wants this page. If a fact here is wrong, the policy may not respond the way you expect when you file a claim.

plain: An insurer's refusal to offer coverage at all, because the risk falls outside what it will accept.
snappy: An insurer's decision not to offer coverage to an applicant, distinct from cancelling or non-renewing an existing policy.
detail: A declination is a no at the front door: the underwriter reviews the application and decides the risk is one the company won't write at any price it's willing to quote. It differs from cancellation and nonrenewal, which end a policy already in force. A string of declinations can push an applicant toward the surplus lines market, an assigned risk plan, or a FAIR plan — the markets of last resort for risks standard insurers turn away.

plain: The slice of a loss you pay yourself before the insurer pays the rest.
snappy: A fixed amount the insured absorbs on each claim before coverage kicks in; higher deductibles mean lower premiums.
detail: If your car repair costs $3,000 and your deductible is $500, you pay $500 and the insurer pays $2,500. It keeps small nuisance claims off the books and gives you a reason to drive carefully. Choosing a higher figure lowers your premium because you're shouldering more of the risk. Health, auto, and homeowners policies all use this tool, though health plans layer on coinsurance and copays too.

plain: A policy where the lawyers' fees come out of the same pot as the settlement — so defence shrinks what's left to pay claims.
snappy: A liability policy structure in which the cost of legal defence is deducted from, rather than added on top of, the policy limit.
detail: Most liability policies pay defence costs in addition to the limit, but defence-within-limits policies — common in professional and management liability — fold legal fees into the same bucket as any settlement. A long, expensive defence can erode the limit before a dollar reaches the claimant, which is why these are nicknamed burning or eroding limits. Buyers of this structure size their limits with the cost of fighting a claim, not just losing it, firmly in mind.

plain: The cleared buffer around a home in wildfire country that insurers increasingly require for coverage.
snappy: A maintained, vegetation-cleared zone around a structure reducing wildfire risk, often required for coverage in fire-prone areas.
detail: In wildfire-prone regions, defensible space — clearing brush, trimming trees, and using fire-resistant materials in a buffer around the house — is the difference between a home that survives an ember storm and one that doesn't. Insurers now inspect for it and may decline, non-renew, or surcharge homes without it. As wildfire losses mount, this once-voluntary practice has become a condition of staying insurable in much of the West.

plain: An annuity that grows your money tax-deferred for years before income payments begin.
snappy: An annuity with an accumulation phase that builds value tax-deferred, with income or withdrawals starting at a later date.
detail: A deferred annuity has two lives: an accumulation phase where the money grows tax-deferred, then a payout phase that can begin years later through annuitization or withdrawals. Fixed, indexed, and variable versions differ by how the value grows. Savers use them as a tax-deferred supplement to retirement accounts, but surrender charges lock the money up early on and gains are taxed as ordinary income when taken.

plain: A plan that helps pay for cleanings, fillings, and bigger dental work, usually with a low annual cap.
snappy: Coverage for dental care, typically with full preventive cleanings but a low annual maximum on major work.
detail: Dental insurance works differently from medical: it usually covers preventive cleanings fully, basic work like fillings at a share, and major work like crowns at half — all under a low annual maximum, often around $1,500. Hit the cap and you pay the rest yourself. It's commonly sold as a standalone or employer add-on, and the modest limits mean it cushions routine care more than it protects against catastrophe.

plain: The state agency that licenses and polices insurers and handles consumer complaints.
snappy: A state government agency that regulates insurers and agents, oversees solvency and conduct, and assists consumers.
detail: Every state has a department of insurance — the agency, led by the insurance commissioner, that turns insurance regulation into daily practice. It licenses companies and producers, reviews rate and form filings, conducts financial and market conduct examinations, and runs the consumer-complaint line where policyholders dispute claims and cancellations. Its filings and complaint data are public, making it the first stop both for checking whether an insurer is licensed and for escalating a grievance the insurer won't resolve.

plain: The drop in an item's value as it ages and wears — subtracted when a policy pays actual cash value.
snappy: The decline in property value from age, wear, and obsolescence, deducted from replacement cost to reach actual cash value.
detail: A claims adjuster paying actual cash value depreciates your loss: a sofa half through its useful life is paid at roughly half its new price. The recoverable portion is what a replacement-cost policy holds back and releases once you rebuild. Arguments over how fast a roof or appliance wears are among the most common sticking points in property claims.

plain: The drop in a car's resale worth after it's been in an accident, even once perfectly repaired.
snappy: The loss in a vehicle's market value after a repaired accident, sometimes recoverable as a claim against the at-fault driver.
detail: Even a flawless repair can't erase a crash from a car's history, so a repaired vehicle sells for less — that gap is diminished value. In many states you can claim it from the at-fault driver's insurer, though your own insurer usually won't pay it on a first-party claim. Proving the amount takes an appraisal. It surprises owners who assumed a good repair made them whole.

plain: An insurer that sells straight to the public — through its own agents, phone, or website — skipping independent intermediaries.
snappy: An insurer that distributes its policies directly through employees or its own channels rather than independent agents or brokers.
detail: A direct writer cuts out the independent middleman: it reaches customers through its own captive agents, call centres, or website rather than independent agencies, and keeps the distribution cost it would otherwise pay away. The big personal-lines brands built their scale and lower expense ratio this way, often passing some of the saving to price. The contrast is the independent agency model, where unaffiliated agents and brokers place business across many carriers. The two systems have competed for over a century.

plain: Selling insurance straight to the buyer online or by phone, with no agent in the middle.
snappy: A distribution model in which insurers sell coverage directly to consumers through digital and phone channels without intermediaries.
detail: Direct-to-consumer distribution lets a buyer get a quote and bind a policy on a website or app with no human producer involved, the model heavy advertising has made familiar in auto insurance. It strips out commission and speeds the purchase, suiting simple, standardized products. It overlaps with the direct writer model and with insurtech, and it works best where coverage is easy to compare; complex commercial and life risks still tend to need the guidance an agent or broker provides.

plain: Coverage that protects a company's board and executives personally when they're sued over how they ran the business.
snappy: Coverage for the personal liability of directors and officers arising from decisions made in their corporate roles.
detail: Directors and officers insurance shields the people who steer a company from claims that they breached their duties — shareholders alleging a bad merger, regulators questioning disclosures, employees or competitors suing the leadership. It protects executives' personal assets when the company can't or won't indemnify them, and reimburses the company when it does. Any business seeking outside investors or a capable board effectively must carry it, since few directors will serve without the protection.

plain: Income protection that pays you part of your paycheck if illness or injury keeps you from working.
snappy: Coverage replacing a portion of earned income when illness or injury prevents the insured from working.
detail: Disability insurance protects the asset most people forget — their ability to earn. Short-term policies cover weeks to months; long-term ones can pay to retirement age, typically replacing 50–70% of income after an elimination period. Employers often provide a base layer, which workers supplement individually. It matters most for those whose savings couldn't survive a year off work, and the definition of "disabled" in the policy decides whether a claim pays.

plain: Spreading risk across many types, places, and lines so no single event can sink the whole book.
snappy: Spreading exposures across uncorrelated risks, regions, and lines so that a single event cannot threaten the whole portfolio.
detail: Diversification is risk pooling's strategic layer: an insurer that writes only coastal homeowners is one hurricane from ruin, but one spread across regions, perils, and lines of business survives any single shock. The goal is uncorrelated exposures — risks that don't all fail together — so a bad year in one corner is offset elsewhere. Reinsurance and geographic spread are the main tools, and the lack of diversification is what makes catastrophe and accumulation risk so dangerous.

plain: A yearly payment some life policies return to owners when the insurer does better than expected.
snappy: A return of surplus paid to owners of a participating policy when the insurer does better than its conservative pricing assumed.
detail: A mutual insurer prices participating whole life conservatively, then returns the surplus as an annual dividend when claims, expenses, and investments come in better than assumed. It isn't guaranteed. Owners can take it as cash, use it to cut premiums, or buy paid-up additions that grow the death benefit and cash value. Dividends are treated as a return of premium for tax purposes until they exceed what you paid in.

plain: Homeowner coverage for injuries your dog causes — a major and rising share of liability claims.
snappy: Liability coverage paying for injuries caused by a dog the policyholder owns, a leading driver of homeowners liability claims.
detail: Dog bites and related injuries are one of the largest categories of homeowners liability claims, costing insurers over a billion dollars a year. Personal liability coverage typically pays, but insurers respond by surcharging, excluding certain breeds, or refusing to cover a dog with a bite history. A serious bite claim can exhaust the standard liability limit, another reason owners with dogs are urged to carry an umbrella policy.

plain: Driving drunk or drugged — a conviction that sends car insurance costs soaring or gets you dropped.
snappy: A conviction for operating a vehicle while impaired, treated by insurers as a major red flag that sharply raises premiums.
detail: A DUI is among the costliest marks on a driving record. After a conviction, insurers surcharge heavily — often doubling or tripling the premium — may refuse to renew, and frequently require an SR-22 filing for years, pushing many drivers into the nonstandard market. The violation typically affects rates for three to five years or longer. It's the offense that most reliably turns a standard driver into a high-risk one.

plain: The legal obligation to act with reasonable caution so you don't foreseeably harm others.
snappy: A legal obligation requiring a person or business to exercise reasonable care to avoid foreseeably harming others.
detail: Duty of care is the first question in any negligence claim: did the defendant owe the plaintiff an obligation to be careful? A shopkeeper owes it to customers, a driver to others on the road, a doctor to patients. Once a duty exists, the law measures whether it was breached. Businesses manage their duty of care through safety programs and signage, and their liability insurance stands behind them when, despite the effort, someone is harmed.

plain: The promise by your insurer to hire and pay lawyers to fight a covered lawsuit against you.
snappy: An obligation on a liability insurer to provide and fund a legal defence for claims that potentially fall within coverage.
detail: The duty to defend is broader than the duty to pay: an insurer must defend a lawsuit if any allegation might be covered, even if it later proves it owes nothing. Defence costs often dwarf the eventual settlement, so this promise is a big part of a liability policy's value. Refuse to defend wrongly and the insurer risks a bad-faith judgment far above the policy limit.

plain: Your obligation after a loss to limit further damage — like tarping a roof — or the insurer can refuse the avoidable part.
snappy: The insured's obligation to take reasonable steps to prevent further damage after a loss, with costs usually reimbursed.
detail: Policies require the insured to act reasonably after a loss to keep it from getting worse: tarp the open roof, shut the water main, move salvageable stock. The duty to mitigate means damage that proper care would have prevented may not be covered, while the reasonable cost of mitigation usually is. It reflects the bargain that insurance covers misfortune, not neglect compounding it. Documenting the emergency steps taken — and their cost — is how policyholders both comply and get reimbursed.

plain: An insurer's obligation to accept a reasonable settlement within the policy limit — failing to can make it pay the excess.
snappy: A liability insurer's obligation to settle a claim within policy limits when it reasonably can, protecting the insured from an excess judgment.
detail: When a liability claim could exceed the policy limit, the insurer controlling the defence owes its policyholder a duty to settle: if a reasonable offer within the limit is on the table, it must seriously consider accepting it. Gambling on trial to save money and instead drawing an excess verdict above the limit can expose the insurer to bad faith and leave it owing the whole judgment, not just the limit. The duty keeps the insurer from risking the insured's assets to protect its own.

plain: The part of a home policy that pays to rebuild the house itself after a covered disaster.
snappy: The homeowners coverage paying to repair or rebuild the physical structure of the home, up to its limit.
detail: Dwelling coverage is the core of a homeowners policy, paying to rebuild the house and attached structures after a fire, storm, or other covered peril. Its limit should reflect the cost to rebuild, not the market price or mortgage balance, which is why underinsurance is so common. Other coverages (personal property, liability) are often set as a percentage of this number, so getting it right matters most.

plain: The slice of premium an insurer has truly earned because that part of the coverage period has already passed.
snappy: The portion of a prepaid premium an insurer has earned as time elapses, recognised as revenue over the policy period.
detail: Pay $1,200 for a year of cover and after one month the insurer has earned $100; the other $1,100 is unearned premium it would refund if you cancelled. Insurers report earned premium as revenue and measure their loss ratio against it. The distinction matters at cancellation and in accounting, where booking premium before it's earned overstates how well a carrier is really doing.

plain: Separate coverage for quake damage, which standard home policies exclude.
snappy: A separate policy or endorsement covering earthquake damage, with high percentage deductibles, excluded from standard cover.
detail: Standard homeowners policies exclude earthquakes, so those in seismic zones buy earthquake insurance separately, often through a state-run earthquake pool. Deductibles are steep — commonly 10% to 25% of the coverage limit — so it protects against catastrophic collapse rather than cracked plaster. Low take-up means many quake-zone homeowners are unknowingly exposed, a gap regulators and insurers keep trying to close.

plain: The day your coverage switches on.
snappy: The calendar date coverage under a policy begins; losses before it are not covered even if the premium is paid.
detail: Coverage doesn't exist until the effective date, which is why buyers time it to the moment they take the car keys or close on a house. Backdating is generally barred to stop people insuring a loss that already happened. Lenders and motor-vehicle offices check it against the purchase to be sure there was never an uninsured gap.

plain: The rule that coverage follows the dominant cause that set a loss in motion, not every link in the chain.
snappy: A doctrine determining coverage by the predominant cause that started the chain of events leading to a loss.
detail: When a loss flows from a sequence of events, the efficient proximate cause doctrine asks which one really set it going — the dominant, triggering cause — and lets coverage turn on whether that cause is covered. If a covered peril starts the chain, the loss is covered even if an excluded peril finishes it. Some states protect this rule by statute, which is exactly why insurers favour anti-concurrent-causation wording to override it. The two doctrines pull in opposite directions on the same facts.

plain: A surveyor's document showing how high a home sits relative to flood levels, used to price flood coverage.
snappy: A certified document recording a building's elevation against the base flood level, used to rate flood insurance.
detail: An elevation certificate, prepared by a licensed surveyor, records how high a building's lowest floor sits relative to the base flood elevation FEMA has mapped. The higher above the flood line, the lower the flood insurance premium — so for homes in a flood zone the certificate can save or cost thousands a year. Owners obtain one to challenge a high rate or a zone designation they believe is wrong.

plain: The waiting stretch after you become disabled before benefit payments start.
snappy: The time between a disability or claim trigger and the start of benefit payments, functioning like a time-based deductible.
detail: On a disability policy, the elimination period is how long you must be unable to work before benefits begin — often 90 days, sometimes longer for long-term coverage. A longer elimination period lowers the premium, the same trade-off as a higher deductible. It exists to keep small, short claims off the insurer and to make you self-insure the first stretch. Long-term care policies use the same waiting-period mechanism.

plain: The part of workers' comp that covers an employer sued over a workplace injury beyond the no-fault benefits.
snappy: Coverage protecting employers against lawsuits arising from work-related injuries that fall outside no-fault workers' comp benefits.
detail: Workers' comp has two parts. The first pays statutory benefits to injured workers; employers liability is the second, covering lawsuits that slip past the exclusive remedy — a spouse's claim, a third party seeking contribution, or injury alleged to be the employer's gross fault. It carries its own limits, often shown as three figures. Together the two parts let workers' comp both pay benefits automatically and defend the employer when someone sues anyway.

plain: Coverage for being sued by an employee — over discrimination, harassment, or wrongful firing.
snappy: Coverage protecting employers against claims by workers alleging discrimination, harassment, wrongful termination, or retaliation.
detail: Employment practices liability covers the lawsuits that come from inside: a fired worker alleging discrimination, an employee claiming harassment, a candidate citing a biased hiring process. General liability and workers' comp both exclude these, leaving a gap this coverage fills, including the legal defence that often dwarfs the settlement. As workplace claims have multiplied, it's moved from a large-employer luxury to standard protection for businesses of almost any size.

plain: An add-on that changes your policy — adding, removing, or tweaking what's covered.
snappy: A written amendment to a policy that adds, restricts, or modifies coverage; also called a rider in life and health.
detail: Add a home office, schedule a wedding ring, or buy back flood coverage and the insurer issues an endorsement that becomes part of the contract. It can expand coverage or quietly cut it, so reading the change at renewal matters. Standardised industry forms mean the same numbered amendment carries identical wording across many carriers, which is why agents quote them by code.

plain: A middle-ground health plan: no referrals needed, but it only pays for its own network of doctors.
snappy: A plan that, like a PPO, needs no referrals but, like an HMO, covers only in-network care outside emergencies.
detail: An EPO splits the difference between HMO and PPO. You don't need a primary care physician or referrals to see specialists, but step outside the network for anything but an emergency and you pay the full bill. Premiums sit between an HMO and a PPO. It suits people who want freedom from referrals but can live within a defined network to keep costs down.

plain: Home coverage for sudden mechanical or electrical failure of major systems — heating and cooling, the water heater, appliances.
snappy: An endorsement covering sudden breakdown of home systems and appliances from mechanical or electrical failure, not wear.
detail: Standard homeowners policies cover a furnace destroyed by fire but not one that simply burns out — that's where equipment breakdown coverage helps, paying to repair or replace home systems and appliances after a sudden mechanical or electrical failure or a power surge. It's a cheap endorsement, not a maintenance plan: gradual wear and neglect are still excluded. Owners confuse it with a home warranty, which is a service contract, not insurance.

plain: The 1974 federal law that governs most employer-sponsored health and retirement benefits.
snappy: The federal law setting standards for private-sector benefit plans and pre-empting state regulation of self-funded plans.
detail: ERISA sets the ground rules for employer health and pension plans — disclosure, fiduciary duty, and an appeals process for denied claims. Crucially, it pre-empts state insurance law for self-funded plans, which is why a big employer's coverage can skip state mandates. When a denied claim heads to federal court rather than a state insurance commissioner, ERISA is the reason. It shapes the legal backdrop of nearly all job-based benefits.

plain: The ten categories of care every marketplace plan must cover — from hospital stays to maternity to mental health.
snappy: Ten benefit categories the ACA requires individual and small-group plans to cover, from emergency care to prescriptions.
detail: Before the ACA, plans could skip maternity care or prescription drugs to cut premiums. Essential health benefits force every individual and small-group plan to cover ten categories — hospitalisation, emergency care, maternity, mental health, prescriptions, preventive care, and more — with no annual or lifetime dollar limits. The rule is why a cheap plan can't simply carve out the expensive things you might actually need.

plain: Short-term coverage for a wedding, festival, or conference against cancellation and accidents.
snappy: Temporary coverage for a one-off event, covering cancellation, liability for injuries, and sometimes weather or vendor failure.
detail: Event insurance is liability and cancellation cover bought for a single occasion — a wedding, concert, trade show, or charity gala. The liability side pays if a guest is hurt or property is damaged, and venues increasingly require it before they'll book. The cancellation side refunds deposits if a storm, illness, or vendor failure scuttles the day. It packages, for a few days, the protections a permanent business would carry year-round.

plain: A formal, sworn interrogation the insurer can require when a claim looks doubtful — lying here can void it.
snappy: A formal proceeding in which the insurer questions a claimant under oath, a policy condition for verifying a doubtful claim.
detail: When a claim raises red flags, most policies let the insurer demand an examination under oath: a formal, sworn, transcribed questioning, usually with lawyers present. Unlike a casual recorded statement, refusing to attend or answer can itself breach the policy and defeat the claim, and false answers can be material misrepresentation supporting rescission. It's a serious tool reserved for suspected fraud or murky losses, and facing one signals the insurer is taking a hard look.

plain: Coverage that only pays after an underlying policy limit is used up.
snappy: A policy that responds above a stated attachment point, paying only once the underlying coverage is exhausted.
detail: A factory needing $50 million of liability cover stacks layers: a primary policy to $5 million, then excess policies for each band above. Each excess insurer pays only when the layer beneath is spent, so its premium is lower per dollar of limit. Towers of excess insurance are how big risks get covered when no single carrier wants the whole exposure.

plain: Reinsurance that pays the slice of a loss above a set point, up to a limit — the workhorse of catastrophe cover.
snappy: A non-proportional reinsurance covering losses above an attachment point up to a stated limit, per risk or per event.
detail: Excess of loss is the layered structure behind most catastrophe and large-loss protection: the reinsurer pays the part of a loss that exceeds an attachment point, up to the layer's limit, while the cedent keeps everything below. A program stacks several layers, each placed with different reinsurers, to build deep protection. It can apply per risk, per occurrence, or in aggregate across a year. Priced as a rate on line, it's how insurers cap their worst-case exposure.

plain: A court award bigger than the policy limit — the gap can fall on the insured, or the insurer if it mishandled the case.
snappy: A judgment exceeding the defendant's policy limit, leaving exposure that may shift to the insurer under bad-faith doctrine.
detail: An excess verdict is the nightmare of a liability claim: a jury awards more than the policy limit, and the insurance runs out before the judgment is paid. Normally the defendant owes the difference personally. But if the insurer breached its duty to settle — refusing a reasonable within-limits offer and rolling the dice at trial — bad-faith law can make it liable for the entire verdict, limit be damned. The risk is exactly what pressures insurers to settle close calls.

plain: A household member specifically left off your policy, whose driving the insurer won't cover.
snappy: A named person barred from coverage under a policy, used to keep a high-risk household member from raising the premium.
detail: Naming an excluded driver lets you keep a high-risk household member — a teen with violations, a relative with a DUI — off your policy so their record doesn't inflate your premium. The catch: if that person drives your car and crashes, there's no coverage at all, leaving you personally liable. It's a deliberate trade some families make, and it must be signed and documented to be valid.

plain: A loss your policy specifically refuses to cover, listed in black and white.
snappy: A clause carving a peril, property, or circumstance out of coverage; the first place an adjuster looks to deny a claim.
detail: Every policy has exclusions — flood and earthquake on a standard homeowners policy, intentional acts, war, normal wear and tear. They exist to keep premiums affordable and to push uninsurable or specialist risks into separate policies. When a claim is denied, the denial letter cites the exclusion by number. Knowing yours is how you discover you need a flood policy or a separate rider before the loss, not after.

plain: The rule that workers' comp is an injured employee's only path — they get benefits but give up the right to sue.
snappy: The legal doctrine making workers' compensation benefits the sole remedy against an employer for a workplace injury.
detail: Exclusive remedy is the bargain at the heart of workers' compensation: an injured employee receives benefits quickly and without proving fault, and in return gives up the right to sue the employer for more. It shields businesses from open-ended injury verdicts and gives workers certainty. Courts guard the boundary — intentional harm or a missing comp policy can break the shield — but in the ordinary case it keeps workplace injuries inside the comp system rather than the courtroom.

plain: The share of premium that goes to running the business — commissions, salaries, overhead — rather than claims.
snappy: Underwriting expenses divided by premium, measuring the cost of acquiring and servicing policies relative to revenue.
detail: The expense ratio captures what insurance costs to sell and administer: agent commissions, salaries, marketing, taxes, and overhead as a share of premium. A lean direct writer may run far below an agency-heavy competitor. Added to the loss ratio it forms the combined ratio, the all-in measure of underwriting profitability. Insurers chase a lower expense ratio through automation and direct distribution, since every point saved is a point that can go to price competition or profit.

plain: A multiplier on a company's workers'-comp premium that rewards a clean safety record and punishes a bad one.
snappy: A debit or credit applied to workers' compensation premium based on how a company's claim history compares to its industry peers.
detail: The experience modification factor turns a company's claims history into a price knob. A mod of 1.0 is average; below it earns a discount, above it a surcharge, all measured against similar businesses in the same class codes. A 0.85 mod cuts the premium 15%, a 1.25 adds 25%. Because contractors often need a mod under 1.0 to win bids, it gives employers a direct financial reason to drive down workplace injuries.

plain: Adjusting a customer's premium up or down based on their own past claims, not just the class average.
snappy: A pricing method that modifies premium according to the insured's actual loss history relative to expected losses.
detail: Experience rating rewards a good track record and penalizes a bad one by blending an account's own claims history into its price. Workers' comp uses it through the experience modification factor; large commercial accounts and group health plans use it too. How much weight the account's own data gets depends on its credibility — bigger accounts with more exposure units get more. It sharpens the price beyond manual rating and gives the insured a direct stake in preventing losses.

plain: The day your coverage runs out unless you renew.
snappy: The date coverage under a policy ends; without renewal or extension, the insured is bare from that moment on.
detail: Miss the expiration date without renewing and you're uninsured the next morning, even if you never meant to cancel. Carriers send renewal offers weeks ahead; ignoring them is the most common way people accidentally let coverage drop. Claims-made liability policies make the date doubly important because reporting a claim after expiration — without tail coverage — leaves old work unprotected.

plain: The statement your plan sends after a claim showing what was billed, what it paid, and what you owe.
snappy: A post-claim statement detailing the billed charge, allowed amount, plan payment, and the patient's remaining responsibility.
detail: An explanation of benefits is not a bill — it's the plan's accounting of a processed claim: the provider's charge, the allowed amount, what the plan paid, and what counts toward your deductible and out-of-pocket maximum. Reading it catches errors and surprise charges before the provider's actual bill arrives. The words "not a bill" are printed at the top precisely because so many people mistake it for one.

plain: How much potential loss an insurer is on the hook for — the size of the bet it took.
snappy: The measure of potential loss an insurer carries, by policy, peril, or region; the base on which premium is calculated.
detail: An insurer measures hurricane exposure as the total it could pay if one storm hit every coastal home it covers. The word also names the rating base — payroll for workers' comp, sales for product liability, square footage for a building — that scales the premium. Managing accumulated exposure in one zip code or one peril is why carriers buy reinsurance and cap how much they'll write in a single area.

plain: The standard unit an insurer measures and prices risk in — one car-year, one $1,000 of property, one life.
snappy: The basic unit of measurement to which an insurance rate is applied, such as a car-year, a unit of payroll, or a $1,000 of value.
detail: An exposure unit is the yardstick a rate hangs on: auto is priced per car-year, workers' comp per $100 of payroll, property per $1,000 of value, life per $1,000 of death benefit. Multiply the rate by the number of exposure units and you get the premium. Counting exposure units consistently is what lets actuaries pool experience across thousands of policies, since the law of large numbers needs comparable units to work on.

plain: Home coverage that adds a cushion — often 25% — above your dwelling limit in case rebuilding costs more.
snappy: An endorsement paying a set percentage above the dwelling limit toward rebuilding, short of a full guarantee.
detail: Extended replacement cost is the common middle ground between a hard policy limit and an open-ended guarantee: it pays up to a set percentage — typically 25% or 50% — over your dwelling coverage limit if rebuilding costs overshoot. It guards against the construction-cost spikes that follow a regional disaster, when everyone rebuilds at once. It's cheaper than guaranteed replacement cost and far more widely available, especially where insurers have grown cautious.

plain: Spending the cash value of your policy to keep the full death benefit as term coverage for a limited stretch.
snappy: A nonforfeiture option using cash value to buy term coverage at the original face amount for as long as the value lasts.
detail: Extended term is the nonforfeiture choice for someone who wants to keep the full death benefit a while longer rather than shrink it. The insurer uses the cash value as a single premium to buy term coverage at the same face amount, lasting until that money runs out. It's often the default option if a policyholder simply stops paying without choosing, preserving maximum protection for a defined period.

plain: An independent outside opinion you can demand when your plan upholds a denial.
snappy: An independent third-party review of a denied claim after internal appeals fail, with a decision binding on the plan.
detail: If the plan denies your internal appeal, external review hands the dispute to an independent organisation with no stake in the outcome, and the ACA makes its decision binding. It's the backstop against an insurer marking its own homework. Patients use it most for denials of expensive or experimental treatments. The plan must tell you how to request it on every final denial notice.

plain: Coverage for the added costs a business spends to keep running after a disaster — like renting temporary space.
snappy: Coverage for the extra costs incurred to avoid or shorten a business shutdown, such as temporary premises or expedited repairs.
detail: Extra expense coverage pays the premium a business spends to stay open: renting a temporary storefront, leasing replacement equipment, paying overtime or rush fees to reopen sooner. It's the active companion to business income insurance, which replaces lost earnings while you're closed — extra expense funds the moves that keep you from closing at all. Service businesses that can't afford any downtime, like data centres and medical practices, often weight this coverage heavily.

plain: The headline amount of life insurance you bought — what the policy is built to pay at death.
snappy: The stated coverage amount of a life policy, the base death benefit before riders, loans, or cash-value adjustments.
detail: The face amount is the number you choose when you buy — a $500,000 policy is built to pay $500,000, the core death benefit. Outstanding policy loans reduce what beneficiaries actually receive, and some permanent policies add cash value on top. Agents size it to income replacement, debts, and future needs. It's the figure on the declarations page that defines the coverage.

plain: Reinsurance arranged one risk at a time — for the big or odd exposures a standing treaty won't cover.
snappy: Reinsurance placed individually for a single risk, which the reinsurer evaluates and may accept or decline.
detail: Facultative reinsurance is retail to a treaty's wholesale: the cedent shops a single, specific risk — a skyscraper, a refinery, an unusual liability — and the reinsurer underwrites and prices that one exposure, free to accept or decline. It handles the risks too large or too peculiar for automatic treaty terms, and it lets a primary insurer say yes to a marquee account it couldn't otherwise hold. The trade-off is effort: each placement is negotiated and documented on its own.

plain: A state-backed insurer of last resort for homeowners who can't get coverage on the open market.
snappy: A state pool providing basic property coverage to high-risk homes that private insurers decline, funded by the industry.
detail: When wildfire, hurricane, or crime risk makes private insurers refuse a home, the state's FAIR plan offers bare-bones coverage as a last resort, with insurers in the state sharing the risk and any losses. Coverage is limited and pricey, meant as a backstop, not a bargain. Soaring enrollment in FAIR plans across California, Florida, and Louisiana has become a warning sign of property markets buckling under climate-driven losses.

plain: A federal office that monitors the insurance industry nationally, though states still do the actual regulating.
snappy: A US Treasury office that monitors the insurance sector and represents US interests internationally, without direct regulatory power.
detail: Created after the 2008 financial crisis, the Federal Insurance Office is Washington's eyes on an industry the states regulate. Housed in the Treasury, it monitors the sector for systemic risk and gaps in coverage, advises on policy, and represents the US in international insurance negotiations — but it doesn't license or supervise insurers itself. Its existence reflects the long tension under McCarran-Ferguson between state primacy and the case for a national view of a business that crosses every border.

plain: Paying doctors for each individual test, visit, or procedure they perform.
snappy: The traditional model paying providers per service rendered, rewarding volume rather than outcomes.
detail: Fee-for-service is the default that pays a provider for every visit, scan, and procedure — simple, but it rewards doing more rather than doing what helps. Critics blame it for driving up US health spending, which is why payers push value-based care and capitation as alternatives. Original Medicare still runs largely on fee-for-service, the benchmark every payment reform is measured against.

plain: A government agency that backs low-down-payment home loans so lenders approve buyers who'd otherwise be turned down.
snappy: A federal agency insuring mortgages for lower-credit, low-down-payment buyers, funded by a borrower-paid mortgage insurance premium.
detail: The FHA insures home loans made by approved lenders, letting buyers qualify with down payments as low as 3.5% and weaker credit than a conventional mortgage allows. In return, borrowers pay a mortgage insurance premium that protects the lender against default. It widened homeownership for first-time and lower-income buyers, and the health of its insurance fund is a recurring policy debate. You'll meet it shopping for a first mortgage.

plain: Coverage that pays a business back when its own employees steal money or property.
snappy: A form of crime coverage reimbursing an employer for losses caused by dishonest or fraudulent acts of its employees.
detail: A fidelity bond protects a business from the inside threat: an employee who embezzles funds, forges cheques, or steals inventory. Banks and firms that handle other people's money often must carry it, and federal law requires it for those who manage retirement plans. It's the employee-dishonesty cornerstone of commercial crime coverage, distinct from a surety bond — here the insurer absorbs the loss rather than expecting repayment, because the wrongdoer is the policyholder's own staff.

plain: Coverage for those who manage an employee benefit plan, protecting them when they're sued over how it was run.
snappy: Coverage protecting plan sponsors and trustees against claims of mismanaging employee benefit or retirement plans.
detail: Anyone with discretion over a company's retirement or health plan is a fiduciary under federal law and can be sued personally for mishandling it — excessive fund fees, imprudent investments, or botched administration. Fiduciary liability insurance covers that exposure, which an ordinary management policy doesn't reach. It's distinct from the bonding the law also requires against outright theft. As fee-related class actions against retirement plans have surged, it's become a near-default purchase for employers offering benefits.

plain: An adjuster who goes out to inspect the damage in person, as opposed to handling it remotely.
snappy: An adjuster who physically inspects losses on site, in contrast to a desk adjuster who works claims remotely.
detail: A field adjuster shows up: climbing onto the roof, walking the burned-out kitchen, photographing the wrecked car. The in-person inspection produces the scope of loss that a desk adjuster, working claims by phone and submitted photos, can't gather firsthand. Bigger and disputed property claims usually warrant a field visit, while small or clear-cut ones are settled remotely. The split reflects a constant trade-off between the accuracy of seeing a loss and the speed and cost of handling it from afar.

plain: The first-pass screening an agent does when taking your application — catching obvious issues before the insurer sees it.
snappy: The preliminary risk assessment an agent performs while taking an application, filtering risks before formal underwriting.
detail: Field underwriting is the agent acting as the insurer's first set of eyes: asking the health or property questions, noticing the smoker's cough or the trampoline in the yard, and steering a risk to the right product before the file reaches a home-office underwriter. Done well, it spares everyone wasted applications and surprises at issue. Done carelessly, it sends the underwriter incomplete or misleading information, which can surface as a coverage dispute after a claim.

plain: A rate system where an insurer can start using new prices as soon as it files them, subject to later review.
snappy: A rate-regulation regime allowing insurers to use filed rates immediately, with the regulator able to challenge them afterward.
detail: File-and-use loosens the regulator's grip: an insurer files its rates and may put them into effect right away, with the state retaining the right to review and disapprove them later. It speeds insurers' ability to respond to changing loss costs, keeping markets more competitive and available, at the price of less up-front control than prior approval. Variations like use-and-file flip the order. The choice between these regimes shapes how quickly prices move when claims costs shift.

plain: A small whole-life policy meant to cover your funeral and last bills, easy to qualify for.
snappy: A small permanent life policy, easy to qualify for, designed to cover funeral costs and final medical or debt expenses.
detail: Final expense insurance — also called burial insurance — is a modest whole-life policy, often $5,000 to $25,000, aimed at covering a funeral and last bills so the burden doesn't fall on family. It's sold with simplified or guaranteed issue underwriting, so older or less healthy buyers qualify easily, but the small face amount and high cost per dollar make it pricey coverage marketed hard to seniors.

plain: A regulator's deep audit of an insurer's books to verify it's solvent and reserving honestly.
snappy: A periodic regulatory audit verifying an insurer's financial condition, reserves, and compliance with solvency rules.
detail: A financial examination is the solvency counterpart to a market conduct exam: regulators, usually led by the insurer's home state, dig into the books to confirm the annual statement is accurate, reserves are adequate, assets are properly valued, and risk-based capital is genuinely there. Done on a multi-year cycle and more often when warning signs appear, it's how regulators catch trouble — under-reserving, inflated assets, shaky reinsurance recoverables — before it hardens into insolvency.

plain: State rules requiring drivers to prove they can pay for harm they cause, usually by carrying insurance.
snappy: State laws requiring drivers to demonstrate the ability to pay for crash damage, almost always satisfied by liability insurance.
detail: Every state has a financial responsibility law making drivers prove they can cover the harm they cause — in practice, by carrying at least minimum liability coverage, though a few allow a cash bond instead. Cause a serious crash while uninsured and the law can suspend your licence and registration until you file an SR-22. It's the legal backbone behind compulsory auto insurance and minimum-coverage requirements.

plain: An independent grade of how reliably an insurer can pay its claims — the score buyers and regulators watch.
snappy: A rating agency's assessment of an insurer's ability to meet its policyholder obligations, expressed on a letter scale.
detail: A financial strength rating is an outside verdict on whether an insurer will be able to pay: specialist agencies analyze its capital, reserves, reinsurance, and earnings and assign a letter grade signalling claims-paying ability. It's not advice on a stock but on the safety of a policy, which matters most for long-tail coverage like life insurance and annuities. Banks, brokers, and large buyers often require a minimum rating, and a downgrade can trigger lost business and even a run on an insurer.

plain: Reinsurance that transfers only a limited amount of real risk, working mostly to smooth an insurer's finances over time.
snappy: A multi-year reinsurance blending limited risk transfer with financing, smoothing results across periods.
detail: Finite risk reinsurance sits near the border between insurance and financing: spread over several years, it transfers only a capped, modest amount of genuine underwriting risk while mainly smoothing the cedent's results and timing of losses. Used legitimately, it manages volatility; abused, it can dress up a loan as insurance to flatter the books, which is exactly what drew regulators and accountants to scrutinize it after high-profile scandals. The test is whether enough real risk actually changes hands.

plain: A 1-to-10 rating of how well a community can fight fires, which shapes home insurance premiums.
snappy: A graded rating of a community's fire-suppression capability that insurers use to set property premiums by location.
detail: Verisk grades each community's fire-fighting capacity — hydrants, water supply, fire-department staffing and distance — into a public protection classification from 1 (best) to 10 (essentially unprotected). Homes far from a fire station or hydrant land in worse classes and pay more, or struggle to find coverage. Rural properties and those beyond hydrant range feel it most, and a station opening nearby can lower everyone's premiums.

plain: The moment you first tell the insurer something happened — the report that opens a claim.
snappy: The initial report of a loss to the insurer, which starts the claim file and triggers the adjusting process.
detail: First notice of loss is the starting gun: the call, app submission, or form by which a policyholder or claimant first reports that an accident, theft, or damage has occurred. It opens the claim file, assigns an adjuster, and sets the timelines for response that prompt-payment laws enforce. Insurers invest heavily in making this step fast and painless, because a smooth first notice shapes the whole claim experience and the speed of the eventual settlement.

plain: Insurance that pays you for your own losses.
snappy: Coverage that pays the insured directly for their own damage or loss, as opposed to liability owed to outsiders.
detail: Collision coverage that fixes your own car, the dwelling coverage that rebuilds your own house, the health plan that pays your own hospital bill — these are first-party. The insurer owes its own policyholder a duty of good faith in handling them. First-party claims contrast with third-party liability claims, where the policy pays someone else you harmed.

plain: An annuity that pays a guaranteed interest rate, like a CD from an insurance company.
snappy: An annuity crediting a guaranteed interest rate during accumulation and predictable payments, with the insurer bearing risk.
detail: A fixed annuity is the conservative choice: the insurer guarantees a set interest rate for a period, so the value grows predictably and payouts are steady. It functions like a bank certificate of deposit but with tax deferral and, often, lifetime-income options. The insurer bears the investment risk. Buyers who want safety and guaranteed growth over market upside pick it, accepting modest returns and surrender charges for certainty.

plain: An annuity that credits growth tied to a stock index, with no losses but a capped upside.
snappy: An annuity crediting interest linked to a market index, protecting principal with a floor while capping the gain.
detail: A fixed indexed annuity ties your credited interest to an index like the S&P 500 without direct investment: a floor (usually 0%) means you don't lose principal to a market drop, while a cap or participation rate limits how much gain you keep. Pitched as the middle ground between fixed and variable annuities, it's complex and heavily commissioned, so the appealing "no losses" story hides real limits on upside.

plain: A use-it-or-lose-it workplace account that lets you set aside pre-tax money for medical costs.
snappy: An employer account funding medical or dependent-care costs with pre-tax dollars, generally forfeited if unused by year-end.
detail: A flexible spending account lets employees route pre-tax salary toward out-of-pocket medical costs, lowering taxable income. The catch is the use-it-or-lose-it rule: unspent funds are largely forfeited at year-end, give or take a small carryover or grace period. Unlike a health savings account it needs no high-deductible plan but doesn't roll over freely. December brings the annual rush to spend down the balance on glasses and prescriptions.

plain: Separate coverage for rising-water damage, excluded by standard home policies and mostly sold through a federal program.
snappy: Coverage for flood damage, excluded by homeowners policies, sold through the federal NFIP or a growing private market.
detail: Homeowners policies exclude flood, so flood insurance is bought separately — historically almost entirely through the federal National Flood Insurance Program, increasingly from private insurers too. Lenders require it for homes in high-risk flood zones. Just a few inches of water can cause tens of thousands in damage, yet many owners outside mapped zones skip it — and a quarter of flood claims come from those lower-risk areas.

plain: A federal map designation showing a property's flood risk, which decides whether coverage is required.
snappy: A FEMA-mapped area rating a property's flood risk; high-risk zones trigger mandatory flood insurance for mortgaged homes.
detail: FEMA maps every area into flood zones reflecting the chance of flooding. High-risk zones — the so-called 100-year floodplain — require flood insurance on any federally backed mortgage, and premiums there run highest. Maps are redrawn as development and climate shift risk, sometimes pulling homes into a mandatory zone overnight. Buyers check the flood zone before purchase, since it drives both insurance cost and resale.

plain: The reinsurance principle that the reinsurer shares the cedent's outcomes, honouring its good-faith claim decisions.
snappy: A doctrine binding the reinsurer to accept the cedent's good-faith underwriting and claims decisions within the treaty's terms.
detail: Follow the fortunes is the trust at the heart of reinsurance: the reinsurer agrees to share the cedent's fate on the covered business, accepting its reasonable, good-faith underwriting and claims handling rather than relitigating every decision. Its sibling, follow the settlements, binds the reinsurer to the cedent's bona fide claim settlements. The doctrines keep reinsurance workable — without them a reinsurer could second-guess each payment — but they stop at fraud, bad faith, or losses plainly outside the treaty.

plain: Expensive coverage a lender buys on your home — and bills you for — when your own policy lapses.
snappy: Coverage a lender buys to protect its interest when a borrower's required home policy lapses, charged to the borrower.
detail: If your homeowners policy lapses while a mortgage is outstanding, the lender protects its collateral by buying force-placed insurance and adding the cost to your loan. It's far pricier than a normal policy, covers only the structure (not your belongings or liability), and protects the lender first. It's a costly trap that catches owners after a missed escrow payment, so keeping proof of coverage current with the servicer avoids it.

plain: An insurer's submission of its actual policy wording for regulators to review before it's sold.
snappy: The submission of policy contract language to a regulator for approval to ensure it is legal, clear, and not deceptive.
detail: Alongside rates, insurers must file the policy forms themselves — the contract language — for regulatory review. The state checks that the wording meets legal requirements, isn't deceptive, includes mandated provisions, and doesn't bury unfair terms. Approved standardized forms are why a homeowners policy reads much the same across companies. Form filing is the quieter twin of rate filing: one polices the price, the other the promise, and together they shape what a consumer actually buys.

plain: Your plan's list of covered medications, sorted into price tiers.
snappy: The list of prescription drugs a plan covers, organised into tiers that set each drug's copay or coinsurance.
detail: The formulary decides whether your medication is covered and how much you pay for it. Drugs sit in tiers — generics cheapest, preferred brands next, specialty drugs priciest — and a pharmacy benefit manager negotiates the list. A drug left off the formulary may need a prior authorization, a step-therapy trial, or an appeal. People with chronic conditions check the formulary before choosing a plan each open enrollment.

plain: A member-based nonprofit that provides life insurance and benefits to a shared community, often tied to ethnicity or faith.
snappy: A nonprofit membership organization providing insurance and benefits to members united by a common bond, with a social mission.
detail: A fraternal benefit society sells insurance with a cause attached: organized around a shared bond — ethnicity, religion, or trade — these member-owned nonprofits provide mainly life insurance and annuities while running charitable and community programs. They predate much of the modern industry, growing from immigrant mutual-aid lodges, and they enjoy a tax exemption tied to their social mission and lodge structure. Regulated as insurers but distinct from commercial ones, several remain sizeable life insurers serving their communities today.

plain: The slice of an annuity you can pull out each year without paying a surrender charge.
snappy: An annual amount, often 10% of value, an annuity owner may withdraw during the surrender period without a charge.
detail: Most deferred annuities let you take a free withdrawal each year — commonly up to 10% of the value — without triggering the surrender charge that otherwise applies during the surrender period. It gives owners some liquidity without fully cashing out. Exceed the free amount and the surrender charge bites on the excess, and any gains withdrawn are still taxed as ordinary income, sometimes with a penalty before age 59½.

plain: When a licensed insurer issues a policy but passes nearly all the risk to a captive or reinsurer behind the scenes.
snappy: An arrangement where a licensed insurer issues a policy and cedes most or all of the risk to a captive or unauthorized reinsurer.
detail: Fronting rents an insurer's licence and paper: a licensed carrier issues the policy a captive or risk retention group needs to satisfy state filing or contract requirements, then cedes nearly all the risk back to that entity through reinsurance, keeping a fee. It lets a captive operate where it isn't itself admitted. The fronting insurer still carries credit risk if the captive can't pay, so it demands collateral — and regulators watch the arrangements to be sure real, secured risk transfer stands behind the public-facing policy.

plain: Everyday shorthand for carrying liability plus collision and comprehensive on your car.
snappy: An informal term for an auto policy combining required liability with collision and comprehensive coverage.
detail: "Full coverage" isn't a real policy type — it's how drivers and lenders describe carrying liability coverage plus collision and comprehensive, often with uninsured-motorist and medical coverage too. It's never truly complete: it still has limits, deductibles, and exclusions. Lenders demand it while financing a car. Buyers should look past the phrase to the actual limits and deductibles, since two "full coverage" quotes can protect very differently.

plain: An arrangement where the primary insurer holds onto the reinsurer's premium as security instead of handing it over.
snappy: A reinsurance arrangement in which the cedent retains assets backing the reinsurer's obligations rather than transferring them.
detail: Under a funds-withheld arrangement, the cedent keeps the premium and reserves that would otherwise go to the reinsurer, holding them as collateral and crediting interest. It protects the insurer if the reinsurer fails to pay and helps satisfy regulators wary of unsecured recoverables from offshore or unauthorized reinsurers. The reinsurer accepts it as the price of the deal, since the credit and the assured payment of claims still flow according to the contract.

plain: Coverage that pays the difference if your car is totaled but you owe more on the loan than it's worth.
snappy: Coverage paying the gap between a vehicle's actual cash value and the loan or lease balance after a total loss.
detail: New cars depreciate fast, so early in a loan you can owe more than the car is worth. Total it, and the insurer pays only the actual cash value, leaving you on the hook for the rest — unless you have gap insurance, which covers that shortfall. It's most valuable on long loans, low down payments, and leases. Dealers sell it at a markup; insurers usually offer it cheaper.

plain: Coverage for an auto shop or valet when a customer's car is damaged while in the business's care.
snappy: Coverage protecting businesses that store or service customers' vehicles against damage to those vehicles in their care.
detail: Garagekeepers coverage protects businesses that take custody of other people's cars — repair shops, dealerships, valets, parking garages — when a customer's vehicle is damaged by fire, theft, vandalism, or an accident on their watch. It fills a gap a standard commercial auto or general liability policy leaves, since those cover the business's own vehicles and premises, not the customers' cars parked in the bay. Auto-service businesses treat it as a core line.

plain: Where your car is mainly kept overnight — a key factor in what your insurance costs.
snappy: The location where a vehicle is primarily parked, used to set territorial rates; misstating it is a form of fraud.
detail: Your premium depends heavily on where the car lives, because theft, vandalism, accident, and repair-cost rates vary by neighbourhood. The garaging address — not necessarily your mailing address — sets the territorial rate. Listing a cheaper location than where the car actually sits is "rate evasion," a misrepresentation that can void coverage at claim time. Students and commuters with cars in two places are common sources of honest confusion.

plain: The main doctor who must approve your access to specialists in a managed-care plan.
