Insurers market it heavily each fall during Medicare's annual election period, and regulators scrutinise how the plans are paid.

plain: The part of Medicare that pays for hospital stays, free for most people who paid Medicare taxes while working.
snappy: The Medicare component covering inpatient hospital care, skilled nursing, hospice, and some home health, premium-free for most.
detail: Medicare Part A is the hospital half of original Medicare, covering inpatient stays, skilled nursing after a hospital admission, hospice, and limited home health. Most people pay no premium because they earned it through payroll taxes, though a deductible applies each benefit period. It pairs with Medicare Part B, and a Medigap policy can cover the leftover cost-sharing. You're usually enrolled automatically once you start drawing federal retirement benefits at 65.

plain: The part of Medicare that pays for doctor visits and outpatient care, in exchange for a monthly premium.
snappy: The Medicare component covering physician services, outpatient care, and preventive care, funded by an income-scaled premium.
detail: Medicare Part B covers what Medicare Part A doesn't: doctor visits, outpatient procedures, lab tests, durable medical equipment, and preventive care. It charges a monthly premium that rises with income, plus a deductible and 20% coinsurance with no out-of-pocket maximum — the gap a Medigap policy or a Medicare Advantage plan fills. Delaying enrollment past 65 without other coverage triggers a lifelong late penalty that catches the unwary.

plain: The part of Medicare that helps pay for prescription drugs, sold as a separate private plan.
snappy: Optional Medicare drug coverage delivered through private plans, each with its own formulary and tiered cost-sharing.
detail: Medicare Part D covers prescription drugs through private plans Medicare approves, each with its own formulary and pharmacy network. Enrollees once fell into the "doughnut hole" coverage gap, now largely closed, and recent law caps annual out-of-pocket drug costs. Skip it when first eligible without other drug coverage and a late penalty sticks permanently. Retirees re-shop Part D plans each year during Medicare's annual election period as their drugs and the formularies change.

plain: A private add-on policy that pays the deductibles and coinsurance original Medicare leaves you owing.
snappy: Standardised private insurance that covers cost-sharing gaps in original Medicare, sold in lettered plan types.
detail: Original Medicare has no out-of-pocket maximum, so a long hospital stay can pile up coinsurance. A Medigap policy fills those gaps, sold in standardised lettered plans (A through N) so the same letter means the same coverage across insurers — you shop on price and service. You can't pair Medigap with Medicare Advantage. The best time to buy is your six-month open-enrollment window at 65, when it's guaranteed issue.

plain: The bronze-silver-gold-platinum labels that sort marketplace plans by how much of your costs they cover.
snappy: ACA plan categories ranked by actuarial value: bronze pays least up front, platinum most, with premiums rising to match.
detail: Marketplace plans wear metal tiers that signal their actuarial value — the share of total costs the plan covers on average. Bronze plans have the lowest premiums but high deductibles; platinum flips it. Silver is the pivot: only silver unlocks cost-sharing reductions, so it's often the smartest buy for lower incomes. The metal label lets shoppers compare plans on the same footing before drilling into networks and formularies.

plain: The least amount of auto liability insurance your state legally requires you to carry.
snappy: The lowest liability limits a state requires drivers to carry, often well below what a serious crash actually costs.
detail: Each state sets minimum coverage — the lowest liability limits you can legally drive with, like 25/50/25. Buying only the minimum keeps premiums down but is a common trap: one serious injury or a totaled luxury car can blow past these limits, leaving your wages and assets exposed. Advisers treat the legal minimum as a floor to clear, not a target, and pair higher limits with an umbrella policy.

plain: A life policy stuffed with so much cash so fast that the IRS strips its tax perks on withdrawals.
snappy: A life policy funded beyond federal limits, losing favourable tax treatment so loans and withdrawals are taxed as income first.
detail: Overfund a permanent life policy past the seven-pay limit and it becomes a modified endowment contract: the death benefit stays tax-free, but loans and withdrawals are taxed as gains first and may carry a penalty before age 59½. The rule, from a 1988 law, stops people using life insurance purely as a tax shelter. Agents test funding against the limit carefully to avoid tripping a policy into this status by accident.

plain: The way being insured can make people a little more careless — because the insurer, not they, bears the loss.
snappy: The tendency of insured parties to take more risk or act less carefully because they no longer bear the full cost of a loss.
detail: Moral hazard is the behaviour insurance can unintentionally reward: once a loss is someone else's bill, the insured may lock the door less faithfully or drive a touch faster. Insurers blunt it with deductibles, coinsurance, and policy limits that keep the insured with skin in the game. It's distinct from adverse selection, which is about who buys coverage; moral hazard is about how carefully they act after the policy is in force.

plain: An attitude of indifference to loss — not fraud, just not caring much, because insurance will pay.
snappy: A careless or indifferent attitude toward loss arising because a person is insured, milder than deliberate moral hazard.
detail: Morale hazard is the lazier cousin of moral hazard: not a calculated decision to take on risk, but a shrug — leaving the keys in the car, ignoring a small leak — because the policy will cover it anyway. The harm comes from apathy rather than intent. Insurers manage it the same way they manage moral hazard, with deductibles and coinsurance that keep a careless insured financially involved enough to still care about preventing a loss.

plain: How often and how seriously people get sick or disabled — the risk behind health and disability cover.
snappy: The incidence and severity of illness or disability in a population, the key variable for health and disability pricing.
detail: Where mortality measures death, morbidity measures sickness — how often people fall ill, become disabled, or need long-term care, and for how long. It's the central risk in health, disability, and long-term care insurance, where the insurer pays not on death but on a continuing condition. Actuaries build morbidity tables much like mortality tables. Rising chronic disease and an ageing population push morbidity costs up across these lines.

plain: The rate at which people die — the central risk life insurers are betting on.
snappy: The incidence of death in a population, the core variable life insurers price and annuity providers bet against.
detail: Mortality is the engine of life insurance: insurers profit when insureds live longer than the premium assumed, and lose when claims come early. Actuaries study mortality by age, sex, health, and habits to build the tables that set prices. The same force runs in reverse for annuities, where longer lives mean more payments. Shifts in mortality — a pandemic, opioid deaths, longer lifespans — ripple straight through insurer earnings.

plain: A statistical chart of how likely people are to die at each age — the backbone of life insurance pricing.
snappy: A table of death probabilities by age and sex actuaries use to price life insurance and value future claims.
detail: A mortality table tells an actuary the chance a person of a given age and sex dies in the coming year, drawn from huge population datasets. It's the raw material for pricing life insurance and annuities and for setting reserves. Improving longevity means tables are updated periodically, which raises annuity costs and lowers life premiums. Every life premium ultimately traces back to a number on one of these tables.

plain: The mortgage insurance FHA borrowers pay, protecting the lender on low-down-payment government-backed loans.
snappy: The insurance premium FHA borrowers pay to protect the lender, charged upfront and annually on FHA-backed mortgages.
detail: FHA loans let buyers put down as little as 3.5%, and in exchange borrowers pay a mortgage insurance premium — an upfront fee plus an annual charge — that protects the lender against default. Unlike private mortgage insurance on conventional loans, FHA's premium often lasts the life of the loan unless the borrower refinances out. It's the cost of the low-down-payment, easier-qualifying access FHA financing provides.

plain: Your official driving record — tickets, crashes, licence status — that insurers pull to set your rate.
snappy: A state record of a driver's violations, accidents, and licence status that insurers use to underwrite and price coverage.
detail: Before quoting, an insurer pulls your motor vehicle report — the state's record of tickets, at-fault accidents, DUIs, and licence suspensions — to gauge risk. A clean record earns the best rates; a recent DUI or string of tickets can triple a premium or draw a decline. Violations typically affect rates for three to five years before ageing off. It's the single biggest driver-specific input to your price.

plain: The price break for buying more than one policy — like auto and home — from the same insurer.
snappy: A premium discount for holding multiple policies, such as auto and home, with one insurer; also called bundling.
detail: Insurers reward bundling — putting your auto and homeowners or renters policies with one company — with a multi-policy discount, because multi-line customers stay longer and cost less to service. The savings can be meaningful, but the bundled price isn't always the cheapest overall, so it pays to compare against separate policies. Bundling also simplifies billing and can ease claims that touch both a car and a home.

plain: An insurer owned by its policyholders rather than shareholders, so profits flow back to the people it insures.
snappy: An insurer owned by its policyholders, who share in its governance and may receive dividends from its profits.
detail: A mutual insurance company has no outside shareholders: its policyholders are its owners, electing the board and sharing in the results, often through a policyholder dividend on a participating policy. Freed from pressure to pay external investors, mutuals can take a longer view, though raising capital is harder without a stock to sell. Many of the oldest and largest life and farm insurers are mutuals. The contrast is a stock insurance company, owned by and run for its shareholders.

plain: The body where state insurance regulators coordinate, writing model laws so 50 separate systems stay roughly aligned.
snappy: A standard-setting organization of state insurance regulators that develops model laws and shared tools to coordinate US regulation.
detail: Because insurance is regulated state by state, the National Association of Insurance Commissioners exists to keep the patchwork coherent. It's not a regulator itself but a forum where the commissioners draft model laws and regulations, set statutory accounting standards, run shared databases, and accredit states' solvency oversight. States then adopt its models, with local tweaks. Its work on risk-based capital, market conduct, and consumer protection shapes the rules insurers actually follow in nearly every state.

plain: The exact person or business written on the front page of the policy, with the fullest rights.
snappy: The party explicitly listed on the declarations page, holding the broadest coverage and the core duties under the policy.
detail: Being the named insured matters when a claim is contested. This party can make changes, receives notices, and enjoys coverage that may not extend to everyone in the household or company. Spouses, resident relatives, or subsidiaries may be covered automatically or only as added parties. Commercial policies often debate who should be the named insured versus an additional insured, because the distinction decides who controls the claim.

plain: Coverage that pays only for the specific causes of loss the policy lists by name.
snappy: A coverage basis insuring only the causes of loss explicitly listed, placing the burden of proof on the policyholder.
detail: A named-perils policy covers only what it lists — fire, lightning, windstorm, hail, theft, and a handful more — and nothing else. The burden sits on you to show your loss came from a listed peril. It's cheaper but leaves more gaps than open-perils coverage, and it's the basis for personal property under a standard HO-3 and for everything under bare-bones HO-1 and HO-2 forms. Reading the list is reading your real protection.

plain: The federal program that provides most US flood insurance where private insurers won't.
snappy: A FEMA-run program providing federally backed flood insurance to communities that adopt floodplain-management rules.
detail: The National Flood Insurance Program, run by FEMA, has long been the main source of US flood coverage, stepping in where private insurers feared the risk. Communities that adopt floodplain rules let residents buy NFIP policies; lenders require them in high-risk zones. Repeated catastrophic seasons have left the program deeply in debt, driving reforms to its maps and rates and the slow growth of a private flood market alongside it.

plain: Carelessness that causes harm — failing to take the reasonable care a situation called for.
snappy: The failure to exercise the care a reasonable person would, which causes injury or loss and grounds most liability claims.
detail: Negligence is the workhorse of liability law: it asks whether someone owed a duty of care, fell short of it, and thereby caused harm. A shop that leaves a spill unmarked, a driver who runs a light, a doctor who misreads a scan — each may be negligent. Proving the four elements, including proximate cause, is what turns an accident into a payable liability claim, and it's the standard most liability insurance is written to answer.

plain: How much risk an insurer keeps for itself after buying reinsurance — its own skin in the game.
snappy: The amount of risk a ceding company retains for its own account after ceding the rest to reinsurers.
detail: Net retention is the line an insurer draws between what it keeps and what it cedes: the slice of each risk, or each loss, it absorbs on its own balance sheet before reinsurance responds. Set it high and the insurer keeps more premium but more volatility; set it low and it pays away premium for stability. The choice flows directly from the company's risk appetite and capital, and it's the first number negotiated in any reinsurance program.

plain: The group of doctors, hospitals, and pharmacies your plan has signed up at discounted rates.
snappy: The set of providers contracted with a health plan to deliver care at negotiated rates; in-network costs you least.
detail: Your plan negotiates prices with a network of doctors and hospitals; using them triggers the lowest cost-share. Go out-of-network and you pay more — sometimes everything, plus balance billing. Whether your own doctor is in-network is the first thing to check before picking a plan or booking a procedure. A narrow network keeps premiums low by including fewer providers, a trade-off buyers often miss until they need a specialist.

plain: Coverage that buys you a brand-new equivalent car if you total a nearly-new one, instead of paying depreciated value.
snappy: An add-on paying for a new vehicle of the same make and model after a total loss of a recently purchased car.
detail: Standard collision coverage pays only actual cash value, so totaling a one-year-old car leaves you short of a replacement. New car replacement coverage closes that gap by paying for a brand-new equivalent — same make and model — usually if the car is under a year or two old with low mileage. It costs extra and matters most to buyers who'd be upset getting a depreciated check on a nearly-new vehicle.

plain: A 2022 law that stops you getting hit with surprise bills from out-of-network doctors you didn't choose.
snappy: A federal law barring surprise balance bills for out-of-network emergency care and certain in-network-facility services.
detail: Effective 2022, the No Surprises Act protects patients from balance billing when they couldn't reasonably pick an in-network provider — emergency care, or the out-of-network anesthesiologist at an in-network hospital. Disputes between insurer and provider go to an arbitration process instead of landing on the patient. It closed one of the most hated gaps in US health coverage and reshaped how out-of-network claims are settled.

plain: A system where your own insurer pays your crash injuries regardless of who caused the accident.
snappy: An auto regime where each driver's own policy pays their injury costs, limiting lawsuits over fault for minor claims.
detail: In no-fault states, your own personal injury protection pays your medical bills and lost wages after a crash no matter who caused it, and your right to sue the other driver is limited unless injuries cross a serious-injury threshold. The aim is faster payment and fewer lawsuits; critics blame it for fraud and higher premiums. About a dozen states use some version, the rest run on the traditional tort system.

plain: Liability coverage for someone who drives but doesn't own a car.
snappy: A policy providing liability coverage to a driver without a vehicle, for borrowed or rented cars or to maintain continuous coverage.
detail: Non-owner car insurance gives liability coverage to people who drive others' or rented cars but own none — useful for keeping continuous coverage between cars, satisfying an SR-22 requirement without a vehicle, or frequent renters who want more than a rental counter's coverage. It's secondary to any policy on the car itself and never covers physical damage to the borrowed vehicle. It's cheap because there's no owned car to insure.

plain: Reinsurance that pays only once losses climb past a set level — protecting against the big hits, not the routine ones.
snappy: A reinsurance structure responding only when losses exceed an agreed retention, rather than sharing every loss proportionally.
detail: Non-proportional reinsurance kicks in at a threshold: the cedent absorbs losses up to its retention, and the reinsurer pays only the excess above it, up to a limit. Excess of loss cover is the main form. Premium isn't a simple share of the original but a negotiated price for the layer of protection, often quoted as a rate on line. It's how insurers buy catastrophe and large-loss protection without paying away a slice of every ordinary claim.

plain: An annuity bought with money you've already paid tax on, so only the growth is taxed later.
snappy: An annuity funded with after-tax dollars, where only the earnings portion of each payout is taxable.
detail: A non-qualified annuity is purchased with after-tax money, so you've already paid tax on the principal; only the earnings are taxed when withdrawn, and an exclusion ratio sorts each payment into taxable gain and tax-free return of principal. There's no required minimum distribution and no contribution cap, which makes these annuities a popular tax-deferral tool for savers who've maxed out other retirement accounts.

plain: The choices that let you keep some value from a permanent policy you stop paying for, instead of losing everything.
snappy: Guaranteed alternatives — cash, reduced paid-up, or extended term — preserving value when premiums on a permanent policy stop.
detail: State law requires permanent policies to offer nonforfeiture options so a lapsing policyholder doesn't forfeit the cash value built up. You can take the cash surrender value, convert to a smaller reduced paid-up policy needing no more premiums, or use the value to buy extended term coverage at the same face amount for a limited time. These guarantees are what make whole life's cash value a genuine asset.

plain: When the insurer decides not to offer you another term at the end of this one.
snappy: A decision by the insurer to end coverage at expiration rather than offer a renewal, distinct from mid-term cancellation.
detail: Nonrenewal isn't a cancellation — your current policy runs to its expiration date — but you must find a new carrier before it ends. Insurers nonrenew after too many claims, or when they pull out of a whole region, as many did from wildfire- and hurricane-exposed states. State law sets how much advance notice you're owed, giving you time to shop before going bare.

plain: A single covered event — like one accident — that the policy treats as one loss.
snappy: An event, or series of related events, that causes covered loss and counts as one incident against the policy limit.
detail: How you count occurrences decides how much coverage you have. One car crash injuring three people is usually one occurrence, capped by the per-occurrence limit; a chemical leak over months might be one occurrence or many, a distinction litigated for millions. Liability policies pair a per-occurrence limit with a larger aggregate limit so a string of separate events can't blow through the year's coverage at once.

plain: Liability cover that pays for any harm that happened while the policy was active — even if the claim comes years later.
snappy: A liability policy that responds to injury or damage taking place during its term, no matter when the claim is filed.
detail: Buy an occurrence policy for 2024 and it covers an injury caused in 2024 even if the lawsuit lands in 2030 — the trigger is when the harm happened, not when the claim arrives. That makes old policies valuable forever and removes the need for tail coverage. It's the opposite of a claims-made policy, and it's why contractors and manufacturers prize occurrence forms for long-tail risks.

plain: Insurance for ships and the cargo they carry across the sea — the oldest branch of the whole industry.
snappy: Coverage for vessels, cargo, and marine liability arising from transport over water, the historical root of modern insurance.
detail: Ocean marine is where insurance began, in the coffee houses where Lloyd's of London took shape to cover ships and their cargo. It still insures hulls, the goods aboard, freight charges, and the shipowner's liability for the voyage. Global trade rests on it: a single container vessel carries values an importer could never absorb alone. Cargo insurance for goods crossing borders is its most common form for ordinary businesses.

plain: Replacement car parts made by the original manufacturer, not a third party.
snappy: Repair parts produced by the vehicle's maker, generally costlier than aftermarket parts and sometimes required by policy.
detail: OEM parts come from the vehicle's original manufacturer and match the factory exactly, but cost more than aftermarket equivalents. Insurers often specify aftermarket or used parts on older cars to control claim costs, while some policies or state laws guarantee OEM parts, especially on newer vehicles. Which parts a repair uses is a frequent flashpoint between owners who want factory parts and insurers watching the bill.

plain: The yearly window when you can sign up for or change your health plan.
snappy: The annual period when people can enroll in or switch health plans without needing a qualifying life event.
detail: Outside open enrollment, you generally can't buy or change individual or marketplace coverage unless a qualifying life event opens a special enrollment period. Employers run their own open enrollment each autumn; the ACA marketplace and Medicare have their own calendars. Miss it without a qualifying event and you're locked out — or locked in — until next year. It's the deadline that drives the annual scramble to compare plans.

plain: Coverage that protects against every cause of loss except those the policy specifically excludes.
snappy: A coverage basis insuring all causes of loss except those listed as exclusions, placing the burden of proof on the insurer.
detail: Open perils — also called all-risk — is the broader of the two coverage approaches: instead of listing what's covered, it covers everything except stated exclusions like flood, earthquake, wear, and neglect. The burden flips to the insurer to prove a loss is excluded. It's the basis for the dwelling under an HO-3 and for everything under an HO-5, and it's why those forms protect more than a named-perils policy of the same price tier.

plain: Home coverage for the extra cost of rebuilding to today's building codes after a loss.
snappy: Coverage for the added cost of meeting current building codes when repairing or rebuilding a damaged structure.
detail: When an older home is badly damaged, codes may require rebuilding to modern standards — updated wiring, hurricane straps, accessibility features — costs a standard policy won't fully pay. Ordinance or law coverage fills that gap, including the expense of demolishing and removing undamaged portions a code upgrade forces. It's vital for older homes, where the code-compliance bill after a major loss can dwarf the basic repair cost.

plain: Home insurance for detached buildings on your lot — a garage, shed, or fence.
snappy: The homeowners coverage for structures not attached to the house, such as a detached garage, shed, or fence.
detail: Other structures coverage protects the freestanding things on your property: a detached garage, tool shed, gazebo, fence, or in-ground pool. It's usually set automatically at around 10% of the dwelling coverage limit, which can fall short for an elaborate detached workshop or barn. Owners with significant outbuildings often raise it by endorsement so a fire that takes the garage is fully covered.

plain: A doctor or hospital your plan hasn't signed up — so you pay much more, or everything.
snappy: Providers without a contract with your plan; care from them costs more and may not count toward your limits.
detail: Out-of-network providers haven't agreed to your plan's rates, so the plan pays less or nothing and you can be balance-billed for the difference. HMOs and EPOs cover nothing out-of-network except emergencies; PPOs cover it at a steeper cost-share. The No Surprises Act now shields you from some out-of-network bills you couldn't avoid, like an out-of-network anesthesiologist at an in-network hospital.

plain: The yearly ceiling on what you can be forced to spend before insurance pays everything.
snappy: The annual cap on a member's combined deductible, copays, and coinsurance; beyond it the health plan pays 100%.
detail: Once your spending on covered, in-network care hits the out-of-pocket maximum, the plan pays the full cost of everything else that year. It's the real measure of financial protection a health plan offers — far more than the premium or deductible alone. The Affordable Care Act caps how high it can go. Hit it after a major surgery and the rest of the year's covered care costs you nothing.

plain: An insurer's own internal report to regulators on the risks it runs and whether its capital is enough to survive them.
snappy: A self-assessment in which an insurer evaluates its material risks and the capital needed to remain solvent under stress.
detail: Risk-based capital is a regulator's formula; an own risk and solvency assessment is the insurer's own answer to the same question. Larger insurers must regularly analyze all their material risks — underwriting, investment, operational — stress-test their capital against adverse scenarios, and report to regulators how they'd stay solvent. It pushes companies to own their risk management rather than just hit a formula, and it gives regulators a forward-looking view that backward-looking statements miss.

plain: Title coverage that protects your own equity in the home, separate from the lender's required policy.
snappy: An optional title policy protecting the buyer's equity against title defects, distinct from the lender's required coverage.
detail: Owner's title insurance protects you — your down payment and built-up equity — if a hidden title defect emerges after purchase, paying defence costs and losses up to the home's value. It's optional but strongly advised, since the lender's required policy protects only the bank. Bought once at closing for a single premium and lasting as long as you own the home, it's cheap insurance against an expensive and rare disaster.

plain: A quick basic health check — height, weight, blood, and urine — a nurse does for your life insurance application.
snappy: A brief health assessment, often at home, collecting vitals and fluid samples for life or disability underwriting.
detail: The paramedical exam is the needle most life applicants remember: a visiting examiner records height, weight, and blood pressure and takes blood and urine to screen for conditions, nicotine, and risk markers. It's cheaper than a full physical and lets the insurer verify what you reported. Simplified and guaranteed issue policies skip it for speed, trading lower scrutiny for higher premiums.

plain: Coverage that pays a fixed sum when a measurable trigger is hit — a quake's magnitude, a storm's wind speed — not on assessed damage.
snappy: Coverage paying a predetermined amount when an objective parameter crosses a threshold, independent of actual loss adjustment.
detail: Parametric insurance skips the claims adjuster: payment is triggered by a measurable index — an earthquake above a set magnitude, rainfall below a threshold, wind over a given speed — and the agreed sum is paid fast, often within days, regardless of the policyholder's actual damage. The speed and simplicity are the appeal, vital for disaster relief and for businesses needing cash immediately. The trade-off is basis risk: if real losses occur but the trigger isn't met, nothing pays, and vice versa.

plain: A life policy that can pay you dividends because you share in the good results of the insurer.
snappy: A life policy, usually from a mutual insurer, that pays policyholder dividends out of favourable surplus.
detail: A participating policy lets the owner share in the insurer's surplus through dividends, typical of whole life sold by mutual companies owned by their policyholders. Non-participating policies pay no dividends but often carry lower fixed premiums. The dividend-paying feature is central to how whole life is illustrated and sold, though illustrated dividends are projections, not promises, and have trended down with interest rates.

plain: Car insurance billed mostly by how many miles you drive, suited to low-mileage drivers.
snappy: Auto coverage charging a low base rate plus a per-mile fee, rewarding drivers who use their car little.
detail: Pay-per-mile insurance splits the premium into a small monthly base plus a few cents per mile driven, tracked by a device or app. It rewards people who barely drive — remote workers, city dwellers, second-car owners — who subsidise heavy drivers under traditional pricing. Drive a lot and it costs more than a standard policy. It's a niche of usage-based insurance aimed squarely at the low-mileage market.

plain: The stage when an annuity stops growing and starts paying income to you.
snappy: The period when an annuity pays income to the owner, through annuitization or scheduled withdrawals.
detail: The payout phase — or distribution phase — is when the annuity delivers on its promise, sending income via annuitization or systematic withdrawals. Lifetime options pay until the annuitant dies; period-certain options pay for a set number of years. The choice between maximising each cheque and leaving something for heirs is made here. For an immediate annuity, the payout phase begins almost at once, skipping accumulation.

plain: The most a liability policy pays for any single accident or event, no matter how many people it hurt.
snappy: The maximum a liability policy pays for all claims arising from one event, separate from the policy's annual aggregate.
detail: A liability policy carries two ceilings, and the per-occurrence limit is the first: the cap on everything flowing from a single accident — one fire, one crash, one collapse — however many people are injured by it. A common structure pairs a $1 million per-occurrence limit with a $2 million annual aggregate. Picking the per-occurrence number means imagining the worst single event the business could cause, then making sure one bad day can't exhaust the year's protection.

plain: Excess-of-loss reinsurance that responds to one large loss on a single policy, rather than to a catastrophe.
snappy: An excess-of-loss treaty applying the retention and limit separately to each individual risk or policy.
detail: Per-risk excess of loss protects against a single big claim on one policy: a factory fire, a destroyed commercial building. The attachment point and limit apply to each risk individually, so the reinsurer pays the slice of any one loss above the retention. It contrasts with per-occurrence catastrophe cover, which responds to many policies hit by one event. Property insurers use per-risk layers to write large individual buildings without betting the company on any single one.

plain: The specific cause of a loss — fire, theft, a windstorm, a crash.
snappy: A cause of loss a policy may cover or exclude, such as fire, theft, wind, water, or collision.
detail: Perils are the dangers themselves; coverage is defined by which ones the policy names. A named-perils policy lists exactly what's covered — fire, lightning, hail — and nothing else. An open-perils or all-risk form flips it, covering every cause except those excluded. Flood and earthquake are the famous ones standard homeowners policies leave out, sold instead through separate programs.

plain: An annuity payout that's guaranteed for a set number of years, so heirs still get paid if you die early.
snappy: A payout option guaranteeing income for a fixed number of years, with remaining payments going to a beneficiary on early death.
detail: A period-certain option answers the fear behind a pure lifetime annuity — dying soon after annuitizing and forfeiting the rest. It guarantees payments for a set span, say 10 or 20 years; if the annuitant dies first, a beneficiary collects the balance. Pairing it with a lifetime payout (life with period certain) lowers each cheque slightly in exchange for that protection, a common compromise for retirees with heirs.

plain: The window of time a business-income claim covers — from the loss until the business could reasonably reopen.
snappy: The time span during which business income coverage pays, running from the date of loss until operations are or should be restored.
detail: The period of restoration is the clock on a business income claim: it starts when covered physical damage shuts a business down and runs until the property is, or reasonably should be, repaired and operating again — not until profits fully recover. Policies may add a waiting period at the front and extend coverage briefly past reopening. Defining its endpoint is the central fight in business interruption claims, since every extra week of restoration is another week of lost earnings the insurer pays.

plain: Life insurance built to last your entire life and build cash value, unlike term coverage that expires.
snappy: Life insurance with no fixed expiry that builds cash value; whole, universal, and variable life are its main forms.
detail: Permanent life insurance is the umbrella over whole, universal, and variable life — policies designed to stay in force for life and accumulate cash value rather than expire like term life. The cash value grows tax-deferred and can be borrowed or surrendered. It costs more upfront, so advisers steer most families to term unless there's a lasting need — estate liquidity, a special-needs dependent, or a business buyout.

plain: Coverage that extends to a friend you occasionally let borrow your car.
snappy: Coverage applying when someone outside the policy drives the insured vehicle with the owner's permission, within limits.
detail: Auto insurance generally follows the car, so under permissive use a friend you let borrow it is usually covered if they crash — your policy pays first. But regular drivers in the household must be listed, not treated as occasional borrowers, and an excluded driver gets no coverage even with permission. Lending your car to an unlicensed or excluded driver is where permissive use breaks down and claims get denied.

plain: Business coverage for non-physical harms like libel, slander, or copying someone's ad — not bodily injury.
snappy: A general liability coverage for offences such as libel, slander, false arrest, wrongful eviction, and infringing another's advertising idea.
detail: Personal and advertising injury is the part of a general liability policy that covers harm to reputation and rights rather than to bodies or buildings. It responds to a defined list: libel, slander, malicious prosecution, wrongful eviction, invasion of privacy, and copying someone else's advertising idea or slogan. A small business sued over a tart online review or a borrowed tagline leans on this coverage, which sits beside bodily injury and property damage under the same per-occurrence limit.

plain: No-fault coverage that pays your own medical bills after a crash regardless of who caused it.
snappy: First-party coverage paying the medical costs, lost wages, and related expenses of the insured after a crash, regardless of fault.
detail: Personal injury protection — the heart of no-fault insurance — pays your own and your passengers' medical bills, a share of lost wages, and sometimes essential services after a crash, no matter who caused it. Required in no-fault states and optional in some others, it speeds payment by skipping the fight over fault for basic costs. It overlaps with health insurance, so coordination rules decide which pays first.

plain: Home insurance that pays if you're legally responsible for hurting someone or damaging their property.
snappy: The homeowners coverage paying for bodily injury or property damage the insured is liable for, plus legal defence.
detail: Personal liability is the part of a homeowners policy that pays when you're sued: a guest slips on your steps, your dog bites someone, your child breaks a neighbour's window. It covers the judgment and your legal defence up to the limit, anywhere in the world, not just at home. Because lawsuits can dwarf the standard limit, it's the foundation an umbrella policy stacks on top of.

plain: Insurance sold to individuals and families — home, auto, life — rather than to businesses.
snappy: The category of insurance covering individuals and households, typically standardized products like home, auto, and personal liability.
detail: Personal lines covers people in their private lives: the homeowners, auto, renters, umbrella, and life policies a family buys. The products are largely standardized and filed with regulators, priced by rating factors fed into actuarial models, and sold in volume. It's the mirror image of commercial lines, which insures businesses with negotiated, hand-underwritten terms. An agent's licence and a carrier's appetite often specialize in one side or the other.

plain: Home insurance for your belongings — furniture, clothes, electronics — if they're stolen or destroyed.
snappy: The homeowners coverage for the contents of a home, typically set as a percentage of the dwelling limit.
detail: Personal property coverage, also called contents coverage, pays for your stuff: furniture, clothing, electronics, appliances. It's usually 50% to 70% of the dwelling limit and follows your belongings even away from home. Valuables like jewellery, art, and guns carry low sub-limits, so owners schedule them separately for full protection. Whether it pays replacement cost or actual cash value makes a big difference after a total loss.

plain: The middleman that runs your plan's drug coverage and haggles prices with drugmakers.
snappy: A company that administers prescription drug benefits, builds formularies, and negotiates rebates with manufacturers.
detail: Pharmacy benefit managers sit between insurers, pharmacies, and drugmakers, deciding which drugs land on the formulary and extracting rebates in exchange for placement. The big three control most US prescriptions, and critics blame their opaque rebate model for high list prices. You never deal with one directly, but a pharmacy benefit manager shapes what you pay at the counter and which drugs your plan prefers.

plain: A tangible condition that makes a loss more likely or worse — frayed wiring, an icy walk, a wood-frame building.
snappy: A physical condition of a property, person, or operation that increases the chance or severity of a loss.
detail: A physical hazard is something an underwriter can point to: a cluttered fire exit, an old roof, a swimming pool without a fence, a factory storing flammables. Unlike a moral or morale hazard, which lives in attitude and behaviour, a physical hazard is a condition of the world that raises the odds or the size of a loss. Inspections, photos, and loss control reports exist largely to find and price these tangible dangers.

plain: The written contract that spells out exactly what your insurance covers, what it won't, and what you both must do.
snappy: The legal contract between insurer and insured setting out coverage, limits, exclusions, conditions, and the premium owed.
detail: A policy is the rulebook for the whole relationship. It bundles the declarations page (your specifics), the insuring agreement (the promise to pay), exclusions (the gaps), conditions (your duties), and definitions. When an adjuster says "it's not covered," they are reading this document. Disputes over a denied claim almost always come down to a clause buried in the policy that one side read differently than the other.

plain: The most your insurer will pay for a covered loss, no matter how big the actual bill.
snappy: The maximum the insurer will pay under a coverage, per claim or in aggregate; losses above it fall back on the insured.
detail: If your liability limit is $300,000 and a court awards $500,000, you personally owe the $200,000 gap — the reason people buy umbrella insurance to stack a higher limit on top. Limits come in flavours: per-occurrence caps each event, while an aggregate limit caps the total a policy pays over its term. Choosing limits is the single biggest lever on both your premium and your protection.

plain: Borrowing against the cash value of your life insurance, using the policy itself as collateral.
snappy: A loan from the insurer secured by the cash value of a permanent policy, charged interest and reducing the death benefit if unpaid.
detail: A policy loan lets you borrow against your life insurance cash value without a credit check, since the policy is the collateral. There's no repayment schedule, but unpaid interest compounds and any outstanding balance is subtracted from the death benefit when you die. Borrow too much and the policy can lapse, triggering a surprise tax bill on the gains. It's a flexible cash source that quietly erodes coverage if neglected.

plain: The window of time your coverage is active — usually six months or a year.
snappy: The span between the effective and expiration dates of a policy during which covered losses are eligible for payment.
detail: A loss has to happen inside the policy period to be covered — or, for claims-made policies, be reported inside it. Auto policies often run six months, homeowners and commercial policies a year. The renewal that arrives before expiration starts a fresh period, sometimes at a new rate. Gaps between periods are dangerous: a single uninsured day can void a mortgage or leave a crash uncovered.

plain: The person who owns the insurance policy and pays the premiums.
snappy: The party who owns the contract, pays the premium, and holds the rights to renew, cancel, or change it.
detail: Policyholder and insured often describe the same person, but not always — a company can be the policyholder of a group life plan covering its employees, who are the insureds. In a mutual insurer the policyholders are also the owners and may receive dividends. When commentators talk about "policyholder-friendly" states, they mean places where regulation tilts toward consumers in disputes over claims and rates.

plain: A share of a mutual insurer's or participating policy's surplus returned to policyholders — a refund, not a stock dividend.
snappy: A distribution of surplus returned to owners of participating policies, common in mutual insurers, refunding part of the premium.
detail: A policyholder dividend returns good results to the people insured: when a mutual insurer or a participating policy earns more than it needed for claims and expenses, it pays part of the surplus back to policyholders. It's effectively a premium refund, not a guaranteed return, and on whole life insurance it can be taken as cash, used to cut the premium, or buy more coverage. It's the mechanism by which policyholder-ownership in a mutual actually reaches the policyholder's pocket.

plain: An insurer's net worth — assets minus liabilities — and the cushion standing between its policyholders and insolvency.
snappy: The amount by which an insurer's admitted assets exceed its liabilities, representing its capital buffer against losses.
detail: Policyholder surplus is an insurer's equity by another name: what's left after subtracting liabilities, chiefly its loss reserves, from its admitted assets. It's the buffer that absorbs a bad year — a catastrophe, an adverse reserve development — before the company can't pay claims. Regulators watch how premiums written compare to surplus, since writing too much business on too thin a cushion is a classic path to trouble. A growing surplus signals strength; a shrinking one draws scrutiny.

plain: Coverage for businesses operating abroad against losses from government action — expropriation, war, currency blocks.
snappy: Coverage protecting foreign investments and operations against political events like expropriation, civil unrest, or currency inconvertibility.
detail: A company that builds a factory or invests overseas faces risks no commercial policy covers: a government seizing the asset, a war destroying it, or new rules blocking profits from being converted and sent home. Political risk insurance covers these, sold by specialist insurers and public agencies. It's what lets banks finance projects in unstable regions, since the lender knows a coup or expropriation won't simply erase the collateral.

plain: Coverage for the cleanup and lawsuits when a business contaminates the soil, water, or air.
snappy: Coverage for bodily injury, property damage, and cleanup costs arising from pollution, which standard liability policies exclude.
detail: General liability policies carry a broad pollution exclusion, so businesses that handle fuels, chemicals, or waste buy dedicated pollution liability — also called environmental liability — to cover spills, leaks, and contamination. It pays for site cleanup, third-party injury and property damage, and legal defence under environmental laws that can impose strict, retroactive liability. Contractors, gas stations, manufacturers, and property developers are typical buyers, since a single leaking tank can generate cleanup costs that dwarf the business itself.

plain: A hybrid health plan that uses a main doctor like an HMO but still pays a little for outside care like a PPO.
snappy: A managed-care hybrid: care is routed through a primary care physician, but out-of-network services get partial coverage.
detail: A point-of-service plan blends HMO and PPO features. You choose a primary care physician and get referrals like an HMO, but unlike one you keep some coverage when you go out-of-network — at a higher cost-share. The name refers to choosing in- or out-of-network each time you need care. Less common than HMOs and PPOs, it appears as a middle option on some employer menus.

plain: A health plan that lets you see almost any doctor without a referral, but you pay more for the freedom.
snappy: A plan that covers out-of-network care at a higher cost-share and lets members see specialists without a referral.
detail: A PPO is the flexible, pricier cousin of the HMO: you can see any doctor, skip referrals, and still get partial coverage out-of-network — though staying with preferred, in-network providers costs you far less. Higher premiums buy that freedom. Frequent travellers and people with established specialists often pay up for a PPO, while the budget-minded take an HMO.

plain: A health problem you already had before the plan started — which insurers once used to deny or overcharge you.
snappy: A medical condition predating coverage; the ACA bars insurers from denying or rating individual coverage based on it.
detail: Before the ACA, an insurer could reject an applicant with diabetes or cancer, or charge them far more. Now individual and small-group plans are guaranteed issue and community-rated, so a pre-existing condition can't keep you out or spike your premium. The protection is among the law's most popular features and the hardest for repeal efforts to touch. It's why open enrollment, not your health, governs when you can buy.

plain: Damage that was already there before the claimed event — the insurer won't pay to fix what it didn't cause.
snappy: Damage existing prior to the loss event being claimed, which the insurer excludes from the current claim's payment.
detail: Pre-existing damage is the old dent blamed on the new crash, the long-standing crack attributed to yesterday's storm. Insurers and adjusters work to separate it from the claimed loss, since indemnity restores what a covered event damaged, not what was already broken. Photos, prior inspection reports, and a claims database history all help draw the line. Disputes over it are common, because the boundary between fresh and pre-existing harm is often genuinely blurry on an aging property or vehicle.

plain: Using statistical models on large datasets to forecast who will file claims and how big they'll be.
snappy: The application of statistical and machine-learning models to data to forecast claim frequency, severity, and risk for pricing.
detail: Predictive modeling turns mountains of data — driving records, credit history, property characteristics, even telematics — into forecasts of which risks will cost what. It sharpens both underwriting and ratemaking, letting insurers price more precisely than broad class averages allow. It also raises the stakes on fairness: a model that leans on proxies for protected characteristics can produce unfair discrimination, so regulators increasingly demand to see what variables drive a model and why.

plain: The legal responsibility of a property owner for injuries that happen on their property.
snappy: A property owner's legal duty to keep premises reasonably safe; breach exposes them to injury claims a liability policy covers.
detail: Premises liability is the legal doctrine behind most homeowner and business liability claims: an owner who fails to keep their property reasonably safe — an icy walk, a broken stair, a hidden hazard — can be sued when a visitor is hurt. Personal liability and commercial general liability coverage exist to pay these claims and defend the owner. How much duty is owed varies with whether the visitor was invited, licensed, or trespassing.

plain: The price you pay — monthly or yearly — to keep your insurance switched on.
snappy: The amount the policyholder pays the insurer for coverage, set by underwriting and actuarial pricing of the risk.
detail: Premium is the meter running on every policy. Insurers set it by estimating how likely you are to file a claim and how big it might be, then adding expenses and profit. Miss enough payments and the policy can lapse, leaving you uncovered. On an earnings call you'll hear insurers report "gross written premium" as the headline measure of how much business they wrote that year.

plain: Borrowing to pay an insurance premium up front, then repaying the lender in monthly installments.
snappy: An arrangement in which a third-party lender pays a policy's premium and the insured repays it over time with interest.
detail: Premium finance lets a business or individual carry a large policy without paying the whole premium at once: a finance company pays the insurer up front, and the insured repays in installments with interest, the policy itself serving as collateral. It's common for big commercial accounts and for high-value life insurance, where annual premiums run into six figures. Miss the payments and the lender can cancel the policy to recover what it advanced.

plain: A government subsidy that lowers the monthly cost of a marketplace health plan for low- and middle-income buyers.
snappy: An ACA subsidy that reduces marketplace premiums on a sliding scale tied to income and the local benchmark plan.
detail: The premium tax credit is what makes marketplace coverage affordable for millions: the lower your income relative to the federal poverty line, the larger the credit, applied directly to your monthly premium. It's pegged to the second-cheapest silver plan in your area. Estimate your income too low or high and you reconcile the difference at tax time, which catches many filers off guard.

plain: Checkups, screenings, and shots meant to catch problems early — covered free under most plans.
snappy: Routine screenings, vaccinations, and counselling, which ACA plans must cover with no cost-sharing when in-network.
detail: Preventive care — annual physicals, cancer screenings, immunisations, blood-pressure checks — is covered at no cost-sharing by ACA-compliant plans when you stay in-network, even before you meet the deductible. The logic is that catching disease early is cheaper than treating it late. The catch: if a screening turns diagnostic (a polyp removed during a routine colonoscopy), the visit can flip to a billable service, surprising patients who expected it free.

plain: Your main doctor — the first stop for everyday care and the one who refers you to specialists.
snappy: The general doctor who coordinates a patient's care and, in managed plans, issues referrals to specialists.
detail: A primary care physician handles checkups, common illnesses, and prevention, and in an HMO acts as the gatekeeper who must refer you before a specialist visit is covered. Building a relationship with one improves continuity of care and, plans argue, lowers costs by catching problems early. When you enroll in a managed plan you're often asked to name your primary care physician up front.

plain: The first policy to pay a loss, before any excess or umbrella coverage gets involved.
snappy: The coverage that responds first to a loss, paying from the first dollar above any deductible up to its own limit.
detail: In a tower of coverage the primary policy sits at the bottom and pays first; only when its limit is exhausted do excess and umbrella layers attach. Primary insurers also usually carry the duty to defend. When two policies could cover the same loss, "other insurance" clauses decide which is primary and which is excess — a fight that surfaces constantly in auto and commercial claims.

plain: A rate-regulation system where an insurer can't use new prices until the regulator signs off.
snappy: A rate-regulation regime requiring the regulator to approve proposed rates before an insurer may charge them.
detail: Prior approval is the strictest common form of rate regulation: an insurer must file proposed rates and wait for the regulator's blessing before using them. It gives regulators maximum control to block increases they find excessive — popular in politically sensitive lines like auto — but it can delay needed adjustments and, critics argue, drive insurers out of states where approvals lag. It sits at one end of a spectrum whose looser settings, like file-and-use, trade oversight for speed.

plain: Your plan's sign-off required before it will pay for certain drugs, tests, or procedures.
snappy: A plan's requirement that a provider get approval before a service or drug is covered, used to control cost and necessity.
detail: Prior authorization makes the doctor prove a planned MRI, surgery, or expensive drug is medically necessary before the plan agrees to pay. It's meant to curb waste but is the bane of patients and physicians who face delays and denials for needed care. Insurers and regulators are fighting over how fast decisions must come. A service delivered without required prior authorization is often denied outright.

plain: Insurance a lender makes you buy — protecting the lender, not you — when your down payment is under 20%.
snappy: Insurance protecting a mortgage lender against default when a borrower puts down less than 20%, paid by the borrower.
detail: Put less than 20% down on a conventional mortgage and the lender requires private mortgage insurance, which pays the lender — not you — if you default. The borrower foots the monthly premium until enough equity builds, after which it can be cancelled. It lets buyers purchase sooner with a small down payment, the trade-off being years of extra cost. It's distinct from FHA's mortgage insurance premium, which works differently.

plain: Splitting a premium or refund exactly in proportion to the time used — no penalty.
snappy: Allocation of premium or refund strictly by the share of the policy period elapsed, with no extra charge.
detail: Cancel a policy and a pro rata refund returns the unearned premium based purely on days remaining — fair and proportional. Insurers use pro rata cancellation when they end the policy, but may use short rate, which keeps a little extra, when you cancel. The phrase also describes how two insurers covering the same loss split it in proportion to their limits.

plain: An estimate of the worst loss a property or portfolio would realistically suffer from a single event.
snappy: The largest loss likely to occur from a single event under normal conditions, used to size limits, pricing, and reinsurance.
detail: Probable maximum loss asks a sober question: if the worst realistic catastrophe strikes — not the theoretical maximum, but the bad-but-plausible one — how much would we lose? Underwriters use it to set limits and decide how much exposure to keep, and it drives how much reinsurance a company buys. Catastrophe modeling generates the figure for natural perils. Get it wrong on the low side and a single hurricane can threaten solvency; too high and capital sits idle.

plain: Coverage for the cost of pulling a dangerous product off the market — notifying buyers, shipping, disposal.
snappy: Coverage for the expenses of recalling a defective or contaminated product, distinct from liability for resulting injuries.
detail: When a contaminated food or a hazardous toy must come off shelves, the recall itself is expensive long before any injury lawsuit: notifying customers, shipping product back, storing and destroying it, and the lost sales while the brand recovers. Product recall insurance funds that operation, complementing products liability, which pays for the harm a defect causes. Food makers, drug companies, and consumer-goods manufacturers are the usual buyers of this specialty line.

plain: A maker or seller's legal responsibility when a defective product injures the person using it.
snappy: The liability of manufacturers and sellers for injury or damage caused by a defective or unreasonably dangerous product.
detail: Products liability is the exposure that keeps manufacturers awake: a faulty heater that catches fire, a contaminated food that sickens diners, a tool that shatters in use. Because courts often apply strict liability — fault need not be proven, only the defect and the harm — a single product line can generate thousands of claims. General liability policies fold in products and completed operations under a combined aggregate, and large makers buy dedicated excess layers on top.

plain: Coverage for being sued over the advice or services you sold — a mistake that costs a client money, not an injury.
snappy: Coverage protecting professionals against claims of negligence, error, or failure to perform in the services they provide.
detail: Professional liability, widely sold as errors and omissions, answers the lawsuits a general liability policy won't: a client who lost money because of bad advice, a missed deadline, or a botched service rather than a physical injury. Architects, consultants, lawyers, accountants, and agents all carry it. It's almost always written on a claims-made basis, so the policy in force when the claim is filed responds — which makes the retroactive date and tail coverage critical when switching insurers.

plain: A bonus paid back to the primary insurer when the business it ceded turns out profitable for the reinsurer.
snappy: A contingent payment returning a share of a treaty's profit to the cedent when ceded business performs well.
detail: A profit commission rewards the cedent for handing over good business: after the reinsurer tallies premiums against losses and expenses on the ceded book, an agreed share of any profit is paid back to the insurer. It gives the cedent a stake in underwriting carefully even on risk it has passed along, and it softens the sense of paying away premium in calm years. It's a standard feature of proportional treaties, often paired with a sliding scale commission.

plain: A state rule forcing insurers to acknowledge, decide, and pay claims within set deadlines — or owe interest and penalties.
snappy: A statute requiring insurers to process and pay or deny clean claims within fixed timeframes, with penalties for delay.
detail: Prompt payment laws put a clock on claims: once a clean claim is submitted, the insurer has a set number of days to acknowledge, investigate, and pay or deny it, with interest and penalties piling up for unjustified delay. They're especially detailed in health insurance, where providers waiting on reimbursement pushed for them. The laws give the duty of good faith teeth by date rather than by argument, and they're a frequent basis for complaints to regulators.

plain: The sworn statement of what you lost and what it was worth, filed to back up a claim.
snappy: A formal, often sworn, statement the insured submits documenting the loss and its value to support a claim payment.
detail: After a fire or theft the insurer asks for a proof of loss — an itemised, signed account of what was damaged and its value, with receipts or photos. It must usually be filed within a set number of days, a condition that can sink a late claim. Adjusters use it to verify the claim; a knowingly inflated proof of loss is insurance fraud.

plain: The car insurance that pays to fix what you damage with your car — usually someone else's vehicle.
snappy: Auto liability coverage paying for damage the insured causes to others' vehicles or property, like fences or buildings.
detail: Property damage liability pays to repair or replace what you wreck — most often another car, but also fences, mailboxes, or a storefront. It's the third number in a split-limit policy like 25/50/25. With average new-car values climbing, a low property-damage limit can be exhausted by a single collision with an expensive vehicle, leaving you owing the rest out of pocket.

plain: Reinsurance where the reinsurer shares premiums and losses in the same fixed proportion as the risk it took.
snappy: A reinsurance structure in which the reinsurer takes a set share of premiums and pays the same share of losses.
detail: Under proportional reinsurance the reinsurer rides alongside the cedent at a fixed percentage: take 40% of the premium and you pay 40% of every loss, large or small. Quota share and surplus share are its two forms. Because the reinsurer's fortunes track the cedent's directly, it usually pays a ceding commission to cover the insurer's costs of writing the business. It contrasts with non-proportional cover, which only responds once losses pierce an agreed threshold.

plain: The legally meaningful cause of an injury — close enough in the chain of events that the law assigns responsibility.
snappy: The cause sufficiently connected to an injury that the law treats it as responsible, separating real fault from remote chance.
detail: Proximate cause is the law's filter on the chain of events: an act is only the legal cause of harm if the harm was a foreseeable result of it, not a freak downstream accident. A driver who runs a light proximately causes the crash that follows; a butterfly-effect chain of unlikely consequences usually isn't covered. Establishing it is essential to a negligence claim, and insurers and courts dwell on it to decide which losses a policy and a defendant truly answer for.

plain: An adjuster you hire and pay to fight your own claim — the only kind that works for the policyholder, not the insurer.
snappy: A licensed adjuster retained by the policyholder, for a fee, to document and negotiate a claim against their own insurer.
detail: A public adjuster flips the usual loyalty: hired and paid by the policyholder, typically a percentage of the recovery, they document the scope of loss, build the estimate, and negotiate against the insurer's staff or independent adjuster. They're most worth it on large, complex property losses where the gap between a first offer and a full settlement is wide. Most states license and regulate them, capping fees and barring solicitation right after a disaster.

plain: Extra money a court adds to punish especially bad conduct and deter others — beyond the victim's actual losses.
snappy: Damages awarded to punish egregious or reckless wrongdoing and deter repetition, on top of compensatory damages.
detail: Punitive damages aren't about the victim's losses — they're a penalty aimed at conduct a jury finds malicious, fraudulent, or grossly reckless, and a warning to others. They can dwarf the compensatory award, which is why courts have set limits on how large they may grow. Many states bar insurance from covering them at all, on the theory that letting a wrongdoer insure away a punishment would defeat the point.

plain: The slice of premium meant purely to pay expected claims, before expenses and profit are added on.
snappy: The portion of the rate covering expected losses and loss adjustment expense, per exposure unit, before loadings.
detail: Pure premium is the cost of risk stripped of everything else: expected losses (and the cost of handling them) divided by exposure units. It answers what claims alone should cost per car, per home, per $1,000 of cover. Actuaries build it from loss data, then load on expenses and profit to reach the rate a customer actually pays. Splitting the rate this way keeps the claim-paying math honest and separate from the business's overhead.

plain: A risk where the only outcomes are loss or no loss — never a gain. The kind insurance covers.
snappy: A risk that offers only the possibility of loss or no change, never a profit — the category insurance is built to handle.
detail: Pure risk is the insurable kind: a fire either happens or doesn't, a driver crashes or doesn't, but neither outcome can make you richer. Because there's no upside to chase, the math behaves and the law of large numbers lets an insurer pool many such risks predictably. It contrasts with speculative risk, where you might win or lose, like a stock bet — that's for markets, not insurers, since insuring a wager would invite people to gamble on someone else's money.

plain: An annuity bought with pre-tax retirement money, so every dollar of payout is taxed later.
snappy: An annuity funded with pre-tax dollars inside a retirement plan, where the full payout is taxed as ordinary income.
detail: A qualified annuity sits inside a tax-advantaged retirement account funded with pre-tax money, so contributions were never taxed and the entire payout — principal and gains — is taxed as ordinary income on the way out. Required minimum distributions apply. It contrasts with a non-qualified annuity bought with after-tax dollars. The label decides how the IRS treats every payment, which is why advisers flag it before you buy.

plain: A major life change — marriage, a baby, job loss — that lets you change health coverage mid-year.
snappy: A life change that opens a special enrollment period, letting a person buy or switch coverage outside open enrollment.
detail: Marriage, divorce, the birth or adoption of a child, losing job-based coverage, or moving to a new area all count as qualifying life events. Each opens a special enrollment period so you aren't trapped by the open-enrollment calendar when your circumstances shift. Plans require proof. Knowing what qualifies is how people avoid a coverage gap after a layoff or a move.

plain: A reinsurance deal where the reinsurer takes a flat percentage of every policy — premiums and losses alike.
snappy: A proportional treaty in which the reinsurer assumes a fixed percentage of all policies in a book, sharing premium and losses equally.
detail: Quota share is the simplest proportional treaty: the reinsurer takes the same flat percentage — 30%, say — of every policy in the covered book, collecting that share of premium and paying that share of every loss. It's a blunt, even split that hands the reinsurer a representative slice of the whole portfolio. Cedents use it to relieve capital strain and grow, since ceding premium frees up the surplus that regulators require behind written business. A ceding commission offsets the insurer's acquisition costs.

plain: An estimated price for a policy, based on the details you give the insurer.
snappy: A non-binding estimate from the insurer of the premium for a described risk, subject to underwriting before it becomes a policy.
detail: You give an insurer your age, address, car, or health details and it returns a quote — the likely premium. Quotes are estimates: the final price can change once underwriting verifies the facts and pulls your records. Comparing quotes across carriers is the core of shopping for insurance, but matching the coverages and limits behind each number matters more than the headline price.

plain: Whether a premium is high enough to cover the claims and expenses it's meant to — the regulator's first test.
snappy: The condition that a rate is sufficient to pay expected losses and expenses and support solvency, neither inadequate nor excessive.
detail: Rate adequacy is the question of whether the price actually works: does the premium cover expected losses, expenses, and a reasonable margin? Regulators enforce a three-part standard — rates must be adequate, not excessive, and not unfairly discriminatory — and inadequacy is the dangerous failure, since chronically underpriced lines erode the capital that pays claims. It's why a rate filing must be justified with loss data, and why a string of poor combined ratios prompts insurers to seek rate increases.

plain: The health-and-risk bucket an insurer puts you in, which sets how much your life insurance costs.
snappy: The underwriting category — preferred, standard, or substandard — that fixes a life applicant's premium per dollar of coverage.
detail: After medical underwriting, you land in a rate class — preferred plus, preferred, standard, or substandard — and that bucket, not the headline rate, drives your premium. A non-smoker in great health pays a fraction of what a substandard applicant pays for the same death benefit. Quotes assume the best class; the real offer arrives only after underwriting confirms which one you actually qualify for.

plain: The submission an insurer makes to regulators to justify the prices it wants to charge.
snappy: A submission of proposed insurance rates and supporting data to a regulator for review or approval before use.
detail: Before changing prices in regulated lines, an insurer files its proposed rates with the state, backed by loss data and actuarial support showing they meet the standard: adequate, not excessive, not unfairly discriminatory. Depending on the state and line, the regulator must approve them first (prior approval) or the insurer may use them subject to later review (file-and-use). Rate filings are where the abstract work of ratemaking meets public oversight, and contentious increases in auto or home insurance play out in them.

plain: The price of a reinsurance layer as a percentage of the cover it provides — reinsurance's headline price metric.
snappy: Reinsurance premium divided by the layer limit, expressing the cost of cover as a percentage of the protection bought.
detail: Rate on line is how the reinsurance market quotes price: the premium divided by the limit of the layer. Pay $2 million for a $10 million layer and the rate on line is 20%; its inverse, here five years, is the payback period a reinsurer would need loss-free to recoup the limit. Low layers struck often carry high rates on line, remote catastrophe layers very low ones. It's the single number brokers and reinsurers track to see whether the market is hardening or softening.

plain: The actuarial process of setting insurance prices so premiums are adequate, fair, and not excessive.
snappy: The process of calculating insurance rates that are adequate to cover expected losses and expenses while being fair and not excessive.
detail: Ratemaking is how a premium gets built: actuaries project future losses from historical data, adjust for trends and inflation, load on expenses and a profit margin, and refine the result with experience and class data. The legal standard regulators enforce is that rates be adequate, not excessive, and not unfairly discriminatory. Get it wrong on the low side and the insurer can't pay claims; too high and competitors or regulators push back. It's the central exercise of pricing actuaries.

plain: Any characteristic — age, location, car, record — an insurer uses to calculate your premium.
snappy: A variable, such as age, territory, vehicle, or driving record, that an insurer weighs to price a policy.
detail: Rating factors are the inputs that build your premium: age, gender where allowed, garaging location, vehicle make and model, annual mileage, driving record, and credit-based insurance score. Actuaries weight each by how well it predicts losses, subject to state rules barring some factors. Understanding which ones you can influence — mileage, coverage choices, the car you buy — is how drivers shop their rate down.

plain: Illegally giving a customer part of the commission or a gift to win their business — banned in most states.
snappy: Offering a portion of the premium or commission, or any inducement, to a buyer as a hidden incentive to purchase, prohibited in most states.
detail: Rebating is paying the customer to buy: an agent kicks back part of their commission, or throws in cash or gifts, to close a sale. Most states ban it as an unfair trade practice, on the theory that it distorts competition toward who pays the biggest bribe rather than who offers the best coverage, and that it can quietly amount to unfair discrimination between buyers. A few states have loosened the rules, but elsewhere even modest inducements can cost an agent their licence.

plain: A title given to a salvaged car that's been repaired and passed a state inspection to drive again.
snappy: A title brand for a former total-loss vehicle repaired and inspected as roadworthy, still worth less than a clean title.
detail: A car with a salvage title that's been repaired and passed a state inspection earns a rebuilt title, letting it return to the road legally. It's cheaper to buy than a clean-title car but carries lasting baggage: lower resale value, limited insurance options (often liability-only), and buyer wariness about hidden damage. Mechanics and buyers scrutinise rebuilt-title cars closely, since repair quality varies widely.

plain: State takeover of a failing insurer — to rescue it if possible, or wind it down and pay claims if not.
snappy: A court-supervised process in which the regulator takes control of a troubled insurer to rehabilitate or liquidate it.
detail: Receivership is what happens when an insurer can't be left to run itself: a court hands control to the insurance commissioner as receiver. The gentler path, rehabilitation, tries to nurse the company back to health or arrange a sale. If that fails, liquidation winds it down — selling assets, transferring or settling policies, and tapping the guaranty association to cover claims. The process aims to treat policyholders and creditors fairly while extracting the most value from a failed insurer.

plain: An insurer where the members insure each other, run by an attorney-in-fact on their behalf.
snappy: An unincorporated association whose members exchange insurance contracts with one another, managed by an attorney-in-fact.
detail: A reciprocal exchange is a pool where the subscribers insure one another: each member is both insured and, in part, insurer of the others, with the whole run by a manager called the attorney-in-fact. It's neither a stock nor a mutual company but an unincorporated association, though to a policyholder it functions like any carrier. Several large auto and home insurers operate in this form, valued for its member-owned structure and the operating flexibility the attorney-in-fact arrangement allows.

plain: A recorded interview where you describe how a loss happened — used by the adjuster and binding later.
snappy: A recorded account of a loss given by a claimant or witness, used by the adjuster to establish facts and coverage.
detail: Early in a claim an adjuster often asks for a recorded statement: a question-and-answer account of how the loss occurred, captured on audio. It pins down the facts while memories are fresh and becomes part of the file the insurer relies on. Because inconsistencies between it and later testimony can sink a claim, policyholders are entitled to understand what they're giving — and in serious disputes, a more formal examination under oath may follow.

plain: The held-back portion of a claim, equal to depreciation, that a replacement-cost policy pays once you actually repair.
snappy: The depreciation initially withheld on a replacement-cost claim, released to the insured after repairs are completed.
detail: A replacement-cost policy doesn't hand over the full rebuild cost up front. It first pays actual cash value — replacement cost minus depreciation — and holds the depreciation back as recoverable depreciation. Once you complete the repairs and prove it, the insurer releases that held-back amount. The structure stops people from pocketing a full payout without fixing anything, but it means cash-strapped owners must front the repair before collecting the last, often largest, slice of the settlement.

plain: The illegal practice of refusing or pricing up insurance based on a neighbourhood rather than the actual risk.
snappy: Unlawful discrimination that denies or raises the price of coverage based on the location or demographics of an area.
