detail: Redlining — named for the red lines once drawn on maps around minority neighbourhoods — is denying coverage, or charging more, based on where someone lives rather than the genuine risk of the property. It can leave whole communities unable to insure homes or businesses, blocking mortgages and investment. It's illegal as a form of unfair discrimination, and regulators police it through market conduct exams and data analysis, since proxies like ZIP code can smuggle in bias that pure risk-based pricing would not.

plain: Using your built-up cash value to buy a smaller life policy you never have to pay for again.
snappy: A nonforfeiture option converting cash value into a fully paid-up policy with a lower face amount and no further premiums.
detail: If you can no longer afford premiums on a whole life policy, the reduced paid-up option turns the accumulated cash value into a smaller policy that's fully paid for — no more premiums, a permanently lower death benefit. It keeps some coverage in force without ongoing cost, a graceful exit from a policy you've outgrown but don't want to surrender entirely for cash.

plain: A note from your main doctor that your plan requires before it will cover a specialist visit.
snappy: Authorization from a primary care physician for a patient to see a specialist, required by HMO and POS plans for coverage.
detail: In an HMO, seeing a dermatologist or cardiologist without a referral from your primary care physician means the plan won't pay. The referral is the gatekeeping step managed care uses to control costs and steer care. PPOs and EPOs skip it. Missing a required referral is a common reason an otherwise covered specialist claim gets denied, so patients learn to line it up first.

plain: Bringing a lapsed policy back to life by catching up and, sometimes, re-proving you qualify.
snappy: Restoring a lapsed policy to active status, usually by paying overdue premium and meeting the requirements of the insurer.
detail: After a life policy lapses, reinstatement may require back premiums plus interest and fresh evidence of insurability — a health questionnaire or exam — because your health may have changed. There's usually a time limit, often three to five years. Reinstating is generally cheaper than buying a new policy at your now-older age, so it's worth doing if you can still qualify.

plain: An extra premium that buys back a reinsurance layer's limit after a loss has used it up.
snappy: An additional premium paid to restore the limit of a reinsurance layer once a loss has eroded or exhausted it.
detail: Catastrophe layers often come with a limited number of reinstatements: once a loss consumes the layer's limit, the cedent pays a reinstatement premium to refill it for the rest of the term, in case a second event strikes. A layer might allow one or two reinstatements before the protection is simply gone. The cost and number of reinstatements are negotiated up front and matter enormously in a busy hurricane season, when a single layer can be exhausted more than once.

plain: Insurance that insurers buy for themselves — spreading their biggest risks to other companies so one disaster can't sink them.
snappy: Coverage an insurer buys from another insurer to share large or catastrophic risks it cannot safely carry alone.
detail: Reinsurance is insurance for insurers. A company holding thousands of coastal homes can't absorb a single mega-hurricane alone, so it cedes part of that risk to a reinsurer in exchange for a share of the premium. This lets primary insurers write more business than their own capital would allow, smooth their results, and protect solvency. The reinsurers in turn pass on slices through retrocession, so a catastrophe's cost ends up spread across insurers and investors worldwide.

plain: An intermediary who designs and places an insurer's reinsurance program with reinsurers around the world.
snappy: A specialist intermediary that structures a cedent's reinsurance program and negotiates its placement with reinsurers.
detail: A reinsurance broker is the matchmaker and architect of a reinsurance program: working for the ceding company, they analyze its exposures, design the tower of layers, and shop the placement to reinsurers globally, often syndicating a single layer across many. The biggest — firms like Guy Carpenter and Aon's reinsurance arm — wield enormous influence over capacity and pricing. They're paid by brokerage built into the deal, and their modelling and market access are why most large cedents place treaties through them rather than direct.

plain: One slice of an excess-of-loss program, defined by where it starts and how high it reaches.
snappy: A defined band of an excess-of-loss program, specified by its attachment point and limit, often placed with several reinsurers.
detail: Reinsurance is built in layers, like floors of a building: each layer covers losses between its attachment point and the top of its limit, and several stacked together form a tower of protection from the cedent's retention up to the largest loss it wants covered. Different reinsurers take different layers, and each layer's price reflects how likely it is to be hit — low layers cost more per dollar, remote upper layers far less. Structuring the tower is the core of placing a program.

plain: Money a reinsurer owes the primary insurer for its share of claims already paid — an asset on the insurer's books.
snappy: The amount a ceding company is owed by its reinsurers for their share of paid and reserved losses.
detail: When a ceding company pays a covered claim, it collects the reinsurers' share afterward as a reinsurance recoverable — a major asset on its balance sheet. Because the insurer depends on those reinsurers actually paying, regulators watch the quality of recoverables closely: a recoverable from a shaky or offshore reinsurer is worth less than one from a top-rated firm. Large, slow-paying, or disputed recoverables have toppled insurers whose own reserves looked fine on paper.

plain: A temporary vehicle that lets outside investors back a reinsurer's book for a season and share the results.
snappy: A dedicated, time-limited vehicle through which investors assume a quota share of a reinsurer's business.
detail: A sidecar is a bolt-on pool of investor money that rides alongside a reinsurer: a dedicated vehicle takes a quota share of a defined book, usually catastrophe business, for a year or two, with investors collecting the profit or absorbing the losses. Reinsurers spin them up quickly to add capacity when rates are attractive after a big loss, without permanently raising their own capital. It's a flexible, finite slice of alternative capital, opened and wound down as the market cycle turns.

plain: The company that insures insurance companies — taking on slices of their risk for a share of the premium.
snappy: An insurer that accepts risk ceded by other insurers, providing reinsurance in exchange for a portion of the premium.
detail: A reinsurer sits one layer back from the public: its customers are other insurers, not policyholders. Giants like Munich Re, Swiss Re, and the syndicates at Lloyd's accept ceded risk from primary carriers around the world, pooling exposures across countries and lines so a disaster in one place is cushioned by calm elsewhere. Because they backstop the whole system, reinsurers' appetite and pricing ripple straight through to what primary insurers can offer and charge.

plain: Continuing your policy for another term, usually with an updated price.
snappy: An offer from the insurer to continue coverage for a new policy period, often at a re-rated premium based on recent experience.
detail: Most personal policies renew automatically unless you or the insurer opts out. The renewal premium reflects a fresh look at your claims, credit-based insurance score, and market-wide rate changes — which is why a clean year can still bring an increase after a region's catastrophe losses. Reading the renewal, not just paying it, is how you catch coverage that was quietly trimmed or a deductible that crept up.

plain: An add-on that pays for a rental car while yours is being repaired after a covered claim.
snappy: Optional coverage paying a daily allowance toward a rental vehicle while the covered car is repaired after a covered loss.
detail: Rental reimbursement pays a set daily amount — say $30 or $50 — toward a rental while your car sits in the body shop after a covered collision or comprehensive claim. There's a per-day and per-claim cap, so a long repair can outrun it. It's cheap and spares you the cost of getting around during weeks of repairs, but it only applies to covered losses, not routine maintenance.

plain: Cheap insurance for tenants covering belongings and liability, since the landlord's policy covers only the building.
snappy: A tenant policy (HO-4) covering personal property, liability, and loss of use, but not the building the landlord owns.
detail: Renters insurance — the HO-4 form — is among the best values in insurance: for a small premium it covers a tenant's belongings against theft and disaster, personal liability if someone is hurt in the unit, and living expenses if the place becomes unlivable. The landlord's policy covers only the structure, not your stuff. Many leases now require it, and the low cost makes skipping it a poor bet.

plain: The itemized cost to fix the damage — the document the claim payment is calculated from.
snappy: An itemized projection of the cost to repair or replace damaged property, prepared by an adjuster or contractor.
detail: A repair estimate turns the scope of loss into dollars: line by line, the labour and materials to put the property back. Adjusters build them in standardized software with regional pricing, and contractors prepare their own, so two estimates rarely match exactly. The gap between them is the heart of most property-claim negotiations. From the estimate, the insurer applies depreciation and the deductible to reach the actual cash value first paid, with recoverable depreciation released once repairs are done.

plain: Enough money to buy a brand-new equivalent of what you lost, with no deduction for age.
snappy: A settlement basis paying the full cost to repair or replace damaged property with new, without deducting depreciation.
detail: Replacement cost coverage rebuilds your roof or repays your stolen TV at today's price for a new one, unlike actual cash value which docks for age. Insurers often pay the depreciated amount first and release the rest once you actually replace the item, to keep the indemnity principle honest. It costs more in premium but spares you the depreciation gap after a major loss.

plain: A statement you make on an application that the insurer relies on — and that must be true.
snappy: A statement an applicant makes during the application process that the insurer relies on in deciding to issue coverage.
detail: A representation is what you tell the insurer to get the policy: your age, your driving record, the home's wiring, your health. The insurer takes these as substantially true and prices the risk on them. If a representation is materially false, the remedy is material misrepresentation — possible rescission. Representations differ from warranties, which the older law treated as strict promises whose smallest breach could void coverage; most states now judge representations by whether the falsehood actually mattered.

plain: The insurer unwinding a policy as if it never existed, usually because the application lied.
snappy: Cancelling a policy from inception for material misrepresentation or concealment, returning premium and denying claims.
detail: Rescission is the nuclear option: the insurer voids the contract back to day one, refunds the premiums, and treats every claim as uncovered. It's reserved for material misrepresentation or fraud on the application and is hardest to use after the contestability period closes. Health insurers were largely barred from rescinding coverage over honest mistakes by the Affordable Care Act, curbing a once-common practice after big claims.

plain: A letter saying the insurer will handle your claim for now but might still deny it once it knows more.
snappy: A notice that the insurer is investigating or defending a claim while preserving its right to later deny coverage.
detail: A reservation of rights letter is the insurer hedging: it will investigate, and in a liability claim provide a defence, but it warns that coverage is still in question and it may ultimately decline. The letter must spell out which policy provisions are at issue. It protects the insurer from being deemed to have waived a coverage defence by helping, while putting the policyholder on notice that the duty to defend here is not yet a promise to pay.

plain: The state-arranged coverage of last resort for those the regular market won't insure.
snappy: Mechanisms providing coverage to high-risk applicants rejected by the voluntary market, such as assigned-risk and FAIR plans.
detail: The residual market is where risks the voluntary market rejects still find coverage: high-risk drivers in an assigned risk plan, fire-exposed homes in a FAIR plan, coastal properties in a wind pool, hard-to-place workers' comp in an assigned pool. The coverage is basic and the price high, and the cost is usually shared among all insurers writing that line in the state. It exists so that mandatory or essential coverage stays available even to those no insurer would choose to take.

plain: On claims-made cover, the earliest date a mistake can have happened and still be covered.
snappy: The cut-off date on a claims-made policy before which wrongful acts are not covered, even if the claim is timely.
detail: A claims-made policy with a retroactive date of 2019 won't cover a mistake made in 2018, no matter when the claim arrives. Keeping the same retroactive date when you renew or switch carriers preserves coverage for your whole career; resetting it forward creates a dangerous gap. Buyers of professional liability watch this date as closely as the limit itself.

plain: Reinsurance bought by reinsurers — passing risk yet another step down the chain to spread it further.
snappy: The transfer of risk from one reinsurer to another, allowing reinsurers to limit their own catastrophe exposure.
detail: Retrocession is reinsurance for reinsurers: having accepted risk from primary insurers, a reinsurer cedes part of it onward to a retrocessionaire to cap its own catastrophe exposure. The chain spreads a single disaster's cost across many balance sheets and continents. It can also loop risk back in unexpected ways — the so-called spiral, where retroceded risk circulates among the same players — a danger that surfaced painfully in the London market's losses of the early 1990s.

plain: A plan where the final premium is settled after the period, based on the losses that actually happened.
snappy: A pricing plan in which the ultimate premium is adjusted after the policy term to reflect the insured's actual losses, within set limits.
detail: Retrospective rating gambles on a good year: the insured pays a provisional premium, then trues it up after the term based on actual losses, bounded by a minimum and maximum. A loss-free year yields a refund; a bad one costs more, up to the cap. It suits large accounts confident in their safety, who effectively self-insure the predictable layer while letting the insurer handle the tail. It's the most direct way to tie premium to one's own results.

plain: A pricier term life policy that refunds all your premiums if you outlive the term.
snappy: A term life feature refunding the premiums paid if the insured survives the policy term, at a higher upfront cost.
detail: Return-of-premium term answers the common gripe that ordinary term life pays nothing if you survive: outlive the term and the insurer hands back every premium you paid, tax-free. The catch is a much higher premium for the same death benefit, so the refund is really your own money returned without interest. Advisers debate whether buyers wouldn't do better with cheaper term and investing the difference.

plain: An optional extra you bolt onto a life or health policy to widen what it covers.
snappy: An add-on to a life or health policy that adds a benefit or coverage, the life-and-health cousin of an endorsement.
detail: A waiver-of-premium rider keeps your life policy in force if you become disabled; a child rider covers your kids; an accelerated death benefit rider lets a terminally ill insured tap the payout early. They let one base policy be tailored without buying a whole new contract, each adding a little premium. In property and casualty the same idea is called an endorsement.

plain: Coverage that fills the gap for drivers working for app-based rideshare services.
snappy: Coverage bridging the gap between a personal auto policy and a rideshare platform's coverage while a driver is working.
detail: Personal auto policies exclude driving for pay, while rideshare platforms cover drivers only during parts of a trip — leaving a gap when the app is on but no passenger is aboard. Rideshare insurance, sold as an endorsement or hybrid policy, fills it so a crash while waiting for a ride isn't uncovered. Drivers who skip it risk a denied claim and a cancelled personal policy for undisclosed commercial use.

plain: The chance that something bad and costly happens — the thing insurance exists to manage.
snappy: The uncertainty of loss that insurance prices and transfers; in industry slang, also the policy or exposure itself.
detail: Risk is the raw material of insurance. Actuaries measure it, underwriters select and price it, and reinsurers spread it. The word does double duty: "this risk" can mean a specific policy or building an underwriter is evaluating. Pooling many independent risks makes the average loss predictable even though any single one isn't — the statistical magic that lets the whole industry function.

plain: How much and what kind of risk an insurer is willing to take on, set by its leadership.
snappy: The amount and type of risk an insurer chooses to accept in pursuit of its business goals, guiding underwriting decisions.
detail: Risk appetite is the strategy underwriting serves: a board decides how much catastrophe exposure, how much of which lines, and how much total risk relative to capital the company will carry. That appetite flows down into underwriting guidelines and reinsurance purchases. A carrier with a small appetite for coastal wind cedes more to reinsurers or simply stops writing there; one with a large appetite leans in for the premium. It's the dial between growth and solvency.

plain: Sorting applicants into groups that face similar odds, so each group pays a rate matched to its risk.
snappy: Grouping insureds with similar expected losses into classes so that premium reflects the risk each class brings.
detail: Risk classification is how insurers keep pricing fair within a pool: drivers, homes, or lives with similar expected losses are grouped, and each class is charged a rate reflecting its own risk rather than the average. A teen driver and a veteran sit in different classes for good reason. Done well it curbs adverse selection; done with the wrong variables it shades into unfair discrimination, which is why regulators police which rating factors a classification may use.

plain: The discipline of identifying what could go wrong and deciding how to handle it — avoid, reduce, keep, or insure.
snappy: The systematic process of identifying, assessing, and treating risks through avoidance, reduction, retention, or transfer.
detail: Risk management is the broader craft insurance is one tool within: a business or individual identifies its exposures, then chooses how to treat each — avoid the activity, reduce the hazard through loss control, retain small losses through deductibles and self-insurance, or transfer the big ones to an insurer. A corporate risk manager weighs these constantly, buying coverage only where retention would hurt too much. Insurance is the transfer step, not the whole of managing risk.

plain: Combining many people's risks so the predictable average replaces each person's unpredictable luck.
snappy: The core insurance mechanism of combining many independent exposures so that aggregate losses become predictable.
detail: Risk pooling is the engine of all insurance: no one can predict whether their own house will burn, but pool enough houses and the fraction that burn each year is remarkably steady. Premiums from the many cover the losses of the unlucky few. The law of large numbers makes the pool's average reliable, which is why insurers want many independent, similar exposures — and why correlated catastrophes, where everyone loses at once, are pooling's great enemy.

plain: Choosing to keep a risk yourself rather than insure it — through a deductible, self-insurance, or just going bare.
snappy: The decision to bear some or all of a risk internally rather than transfer it to an insurer.
detail: Risk retention is deciding to pay for losses yourself, on purpose. Every deductible is a small dose of it; a large company that self-insures its routine claims is a big one. The logic is that insuring predictable, modest losses just trades dollars for the insurer's overhead, so it's cheaper to keep them and reserve for them. The art is drawing the line — retaining what you can absorb, transferring the catastrophic tail you can't.

plain: A member-owned insurer that lets businesses in the same field band together to self-insure their liability.
snappy: A liability insurer owned by its policyholder-members, authorized under federal law to operate across state lines from one home state.
detail: A risk retention group is a liability insurer its own customers own, created under a federal law that lets it license in one state and write members across the country. Doctors, contractors, or trucking firms facing scarce or costly liability cover form one to self-insure together. It can write only liability, not property, and it shifts both the risk and the reward to the members. It's a structured, regulated cousin of the group captive aimed squarely at hard-to-place liability.

plain: The insurer's choice of which risks to take on and which to turn away.
snappy: An insurer's active decision to seek out preferred risks and avoid or price up poorer ones within the eligible market.
detail: Risk selection is underwriting's offensive game: rather than just react to applications, an insurer steers toward the risks it understands and prices well, and away from those it doesn't. Marketing, agent appointments, and underwriting guidelines all shape who applies in the first place. The danger is its mirror image, adverse selection, where the applicants most eager to buy are precisely the riskiest — so good selection is about reaching the risks that aren't self-selecting against you.

plain: Shifting the financial burden of a possible loss onto someone else — the core thing insurance and reinsurance do.
snappy: The shifting of the financial consequences of a risk from one party to another, the principle underlying insurance contracts.
detail: Risk transfer is the fundamental move of the whole industry: a person, business, or insurer pays to shift the financial weight of an uncertain loss onto a party better able to bear it. Buying a policy transfers risk to an insurer; reinsurance transfers it again; capital-market tools like catastrophe bonds transfer it to investors. It's one of the four classic responses to risk, alongside avoiding, reducing, and retaining it, and it's the reason insurance exists at all.

plain: A formula that sets how much capital an insurer must hold based on how risky its business is.
snappy: A regulatory formula setting a minimum capital level scaled to an insurer's investment, underwriting, and credit risks.
detail: Risk-based capital ties the cushion an insurer must hold to the risk it actually runs: a formula weighs its investments, underwriting mix, reserve risk, and reinsurance credit to produce a required capital figure. Compare it to the company's actual capital and you get a ratio that triggers escalating regulatory action as it falls — from explaining a plan to outright seizure. Adopted through the NAIC, it replaced crude fixed-capital minimums with a measure that asks a riskier insurer to hold more.

plain: An add-on that covers towing, jump-starts, lockouts, and flat tyres when your car strands you.
snappy: Optional coverage paying for towing, battery jumps, lockouts, fuel delivery, and minor roadside help.
detail: Roadside assistance — also sold as towing and labor coverage — pays to tow a broken-down car, jump a dead battery, change a flat, deliver fuel, or get you back into a locked car. It's a low-cost convenience often bundled with auto policies or sold by auto clubs. The coverage pays for the service call, not for repairs, and heavy use can draw insurer attention at renewal.

plain: What's left of the damaged property after a claim — which the insurer can sell to recoup some of the payout.
snappy: The remaining value of property the insurer pays for in full, which it may take and sell to offset the loss.
detail: When an insurer declares a crashed car a total loss and pays its value, it takes the wreck and sells it for salvage, often to a rebuilder or parts yard. The recovery offsets the claim cost. A salvage title then warns future buyers the car was once written off. The same idea applies to fire-damaged inventory or a sunk boat the insurer paid out and now owns.

plain: A branded title warning that a car was once declared a total loss by an insurer.
snappy: A title brand marking a vehicle previously written off as a total loss, lowering its value and complicating insurance.
detail: When an insurer declares a car a total loss and takes it for salvage, the state issues a salvage title — a permanent brand warning future buyers the car was once written off. A salvage car can't be driven until repaired and re-inspected for a rebuilt title. The brand slashes resale value and makes full coverage hard to get, which is why buyers should always check a vehicle's title history.

plain: What the insurer can sell the wrecked or damaged property for after paying a total loss.
snappy: The amount realized by the insurer from selling damaged property it takes title to after paying a total-loss claim.
detail: When an insurer pays a total loss, it usually takes ownership of the wreckage and sells it — a crashed car to a salvage auction, damaged inventory to a liquidator. That salvage value offsets the cost of the claim. It's why a totalled vehicle gets a salvage title and disappears to auction once you're paid out. Adjusters factor expected salvage into the economics of declaring a total loss versus paying to repair.

plain: Tweaking a commercial premium up or down for specific good or bad features a standard rate table misses.
snappy: A pricing technique applying debits and credits for individual risk characteristics not captured by class rates.
detail: Schedule rating lets an underwriter fine-tune a commercial price for what the manual can't see: credits for a sprinklered building, a strong safety program, or seasoned management; debits for poor housekeeping or a sketchy location. Applied as a percentage swing within filed limits, it personalizes the class rate to the individual risk. Combined with experience rating, it's how two outwardly similar businesses can end up paying meaningfully different premiums for the same coverage.

plain: Extra, itemised coverage for valuables — jewellery, art, guns — that a standard policy barely covers.
snappy: Coverage listing high-value items individually for their appraised value, beyond the low sub-limits of a base policy.
detail: Standard personal property coverage caps payouts on jewellery, furs, art, and collectibles at low sub-limits — a stolen engagement ring might be barely covered. Scheduling those items on a personal articles floater insures each at its appraised value, often with no deductible and broader perils (a dropped, lost ring). It costs a little extra and usually needs an appraisal, but it's how owners of real valuables avoid a painful shortfall after a loss.

plain: The full list of what was damaged and needs fixing — the inventory an estimate is built from.
snappy: The documented extent of damage from a covered event, itemizing what must be repaired or replaced.
detail: Before anyone prices a repair, the adjuster establishes the scope of loss: a room-by-room, item-by-item account of everything the event damaged. The repair estimate is built directly on it, so a scope that misses the soaked subfloor or the smoke in the attic produces a payment that falls short. Disputes over a claim are often really disputes over scope — whether a given crack or stain belongs to this loss or predates it.

plain: An employer health plan where the company pays workers' claims itself instead of buying insurance.
snappy: An employer plan that pays employee medical claims from its own funds, usually with stop-loss cover for large losses.
detail: Large employers often self-fund: they bear the actual claims rather than paying an insurer a fixed premium, hiring an administrator to process them and buying stop-loss insurance to cap catastrophic costs. It saves money and dodges some state mandates because ERISA governs self-funded plans federally. Most big-company workers are in one without knowing it — the insurer name on the card is just the administrator.

plain: Setting money aside to pay your own losses instead of buying a policy — common for large, predictable risks.
snappy: A formal plan to fund expected losses from one's own reserves rather than transferring them to an insurer.
detail: Self-insurance is risk retention done deliberately and at scale: a large employer funds its own workers' comp or health claims, setting aside reserves and often paying an administrator to process them, rather than handing premiums to an insurer. It captures the savings of cutting out the insurer's margin and keeps cash flow in-house, while exposing the organization to a bad year. Most self-insurers cap that downside with stop-loss insurance against claims beyond a chosen threshold.

plain: A chunk of each loss a business pays itself before its liability policy responds — like a big deductible.
snappy: An amount the insured pays out of pocket on each claim before the liability policy attaches, common in commercial cover.
detail: Larger companies take a self-insured retention to lower premiums and keep control of small claims: they handle and pay losses up to, say, $250,000, and the insurer only steps in above that. Unlike a deductible, the insured usually manages the claim within the retention itself. It's a halfway house between buying full coverage and self-insuring entirely, and it signals an insurer that the buyer has skin in the game.

plain: Home coverage for the buried pipes and wires running to your house that you, not the utility, must repair.
snappy: An endorsement covering repair of damaged underground utility lines — water, sewer, power — that the homeowner owns.
detail: Many homeowners don't realise they own — and must repair — the buried water, sewer, and power lines running from the street to the house. When one fails from age, roots, or freezing, the dig-and-replace bill is steep and excluded by standard policies. Service line coverage is a low-cost endorsement that pays for it, including the landscaping torn up to reach the line. It's a small add-on that prevents a nasty surprise.

plain: The agreed payment that closes an insurance claim — the dollar figure both sides accept as final.
snappy: The agreed resolution of a claim, in which the insurer pays a sum the claimant accepts as full and final.
detail: A settlement is where a claim ends: after the adjuster investigates and values the loss, the insurer and the claimant agree on an amount, the insurer pays, and the claimant signs a release giving up further demands. It may be a quick first-party payout for a dented car or a hard-fought negotiation in a liability suit. Most claims settle rather than go to trial, because both sides usually prefer a known number to the gamble of a verdict.

plain: The document you sign to collect a settlement — giving up the right to ask for anything more on that loss.
snappy: A signed agreement in which a claimant accepts payment as full satisfaction and waives further claims for the loss.
detail: A release is the legal full stop on a claim: in exchange for the settlement payment, the claimant signs away the right to seek anything further for that loss, even if injuries or damage later prove worse than thought. Because it's usually final and irrevocable, signing one is the moment to be sure the amount truly covers the harm. In injury claims especially, a premature release for a lowball figure is among the costliest mistakes a claimant can make.

plain: A cheap, temporary medical plan that fills a coverage gap but skips many protections.
snappy: Limited-duration coverage bridging gaps between plans, exempt from ACA rules so it can deny pre-existing conditions.
detail: Short-term health insurance bridges a gap — between jobs, or before Medicare starts — at a low premium, but it's exempt from ACA rules: it can screen out pre-existing conditions, skip essential health benefits, and cap payouts. Cheap if you stay healthy, dangerous if you don't. Regulators have repeatedly tightened and loosened how long these plans can last, wary of people mistaking them for comprehensive coverage.

plain: Life insurance you can get with a few health questions and no medical exam — faster but pricier.
snappy: Life coverage underwritten from a short health questionnaire and database checks, with no medical exam, at higher cost.
detail: Simplified issue skips the paramedical exam, asking only a handful of health questions plus prescription and database checks, so a policy can issue in days rather than weeks. The convenience costs more per dollar of coverage and caps the face amount, because the insurer accepts more uncertainty. It suits buyers who want speed, dislike needles, or have a condition that would slow full underwriting but not bar coverage.

plain: An annuity that pays the most each month but stops the moment you die.
snappy: An annuity paying income for one person's lifetime only, with the largest payments and nothing left to heirs.
detail: A single-life — or "life only" — annuity squeezes the biggest possible payment from a given lump sum because the insurer stops paying at the annuitant's death, with nothing for heirs. It maximises lifetime income for someone with no dependents to protect, but die early and the insurer keeps the balance. Retirees weigh it against joint and survivor or period-certain options that trade smaller cheques for protecting a spouse or estate.

plain: A captive insurer owned by one company to insure only that company's own risks.
snappy: A captive owned and used by a single organization to insure the risks of itself and its affiliates.
detail: A single-parent, or pure, captive is the simplest form: one company owns the captive and it insures only that company and its subsidiaries. The parent gains control over coverage and pricing, captures the profit a commercial insurer would have kept, and can reach reinsurance markets directly. It suits a large organization with enough predictable loss volume to justify running its own insurer. Smaller firms that can't go it alone instead join a group captive to pool with peers.

plain: A ceding commission that rises or falls automatically with how profitable the reinsured business turns out to be.
snappy: A ceding commission that adjusts inversely to the loss ratio of the ceded business, rewarding good results.
detail: A sliding scale commission ties the reinsurer's payment to the cedent's underwriting quality: when the ceded book runs a low loss ratio, the ceding commission slides up; when losses are heavy, it slides down to a floor. It aligns both sides on writing good business, since the cedent shares in the upside of a clean year and the reinsurer is cushioned in a bad one. It's a common refinement on proportional treaties, sitting alongside or instead of a profit commission.

plain: Padding or exaggerating a real claim — the common, opportunistic kind of insurance fraud.
snappy: Opportunistic fraud that inflates an otherwise legitimate claim or shades the truth on an application, rather than fabricating a loss.
detail: Soft fraud is the tempting kind: the loss really happened, but the claimant pads it — adding a never-owned TV to the burglary list, blaming an old dent on the new accident, or fudging a few facts on an application to shave the premium. Because it rides on a real event, it's harder to spot and far more common than outright staging. Adjusters and special investigation units watch for it, since the cumulative drag of millions of inflated claims is enormous.

plain: The phase when insurance is cheap and plentiful, as insurers compete hard for business.
snappy: A market phase of falling premiums, broad coverage, and abundant capacity driven by strong competition and ample capital.
detail: A soft market is the easy half of the underwriting cycle: flush with capital and chasing growth, insurers cut premiums, loosen underwriting, and broaden terms to win business. Buyers enjoy low prices and wide coverage, and the surplus lines market quiets as standard carriers take on more. The good times sow their own end — underpricing eventually meets a wave of losses, capital tightens, and the market hardens. Insurers who priced discipline through the soft years fare best when it turns.

plain: An insurer's ability to pay all the claims it owes — the central thing regulators police.
snappy: The condition of having enough assets and capital to meet all policyholder obligations as they come due.
detail: Solvency is the promise behind every policy: that the insurer will still be standing, with money in hand, when claims fall due years from now. Regulators guard it relentlessly, because an insolvent insurer breaks promises to thousands at once. They monitor it through statutory accounting, risk-based capital requirements, reserve adequacy, and the quality of reinsurance recoverables, and they intervene early when the numbers slip. Solvency oversight, more than pricing, is the core justification for regulating insurers at all.

plain: A chance to change your health plan outside the normal window after a big life change.
snappy: A window to enroll or switch plans triggered by a qualifying life event such as marriage, birth, or loss of coverage.
detail: A special enrollment period opens when life changes — you marry, have a baby, lose job-based coverage, or move. It gives you a limited window, usually 60 days, to enroll or switch outside open enrollment. Documenting the qualifying life event is required. Losing other coverage is the most common trigger, which is why a layoff doesn't have to mean going uninsured until next year.

plain: An insurer's in-house team of fraud investigators who dig into claims that look staged or padded.
snappy: A dedicated insurer department that investigates claims suspected of fraud and refers cases to law enforcement.
detail: Most insurers run a special investigation unit: trained investigators, often ex-police, who take over claims an adjuster flags as suspicious. They pull databases, interview witnesses, surveil questionable injuries, and build cases that may end in a denied claim, an examination under oath, or a criminal referral. Many states require carriers to maintain one and report suspected fraud. The unit is the insurance industry's first line against both soft and hard fraud.

plain: A very expensive medication for a complex condition, often requiring special handling and the plan's pre-approval.
snappy: A high-cost drug for complex or chronic conditions, usually placed on the top formulary tier with tight management.
detail: Specialty drugs — biologics for cancer, multiple sclerosis, or rheumatoid arthritis — can cost thousands a month and sit on the highest formulary tier with coinsurance instead of a flat copay. Plans gate them behind prior authorization and step therapy and often route them through a specialty pharmacy. They're a fast-growing slice of drug spending, which is why insurers manage them so aggressively.

plain: A risk that can end in gain or loss — like an investment. Insurers won't cover it.
snappy: A risk carrying the chance of profit as well as loss, such as a business venture or investment, which is generally not insurable.
detail: Speculative risk is the everyday risk of enterprise: launch a product, buy a stock, open a restaurant, and you might profit or lose. Private insurance steers clear of it, because covering a bet would let people gamble with the insurer's money and would defeat the law of large numbers that pure risk relies on. The line isn't perfect — trade credit and political risk insurance edge into commercial uncertainty — but it explains why you can insure your shop against fire, not against a slow season.

plain: Auto liability limits written as three numbers — per-person injury, per-accident injury, and property damage.
snappy: Liability limits stated as three separate caps: bodily injury per person, bodily injury per accident, and property damage.
detail: A policy quoted as 25/50/25 carries split limits: $25,000 for one person's injuries, $50,000 for all injuries in an accident, and $25,000 for property damage. The structure caps each bucket separately, so a multi-victim crash can exhaust the per-accident injury limit fast. Comparing the three numbers — not just the premium — is how drivers judge whether a policy actually protects their assets.

plain: A state-required certificate proving a high-risk driver carries the minimum insurance, filed by the insurer.
snappy: A form an insurer files with the state certifying a driver carries at least minimum liability coverage, for high-risk cases.
detail: An SR-22 isn't insurance — it's a certificate your insurer files with the state to prove you carry the required minimum liability coverage, usually mandated after a DUI, an at-fault crash while uninsured, or a licence suspension. It flags you as high-risk, raises premiums, and must stay in force, often for three years; let the policy lapse and the insurer notifies the state, risking your licence again.

plain: An adjuster who is a salaried employee of the insurance company.
snappy: An adjuster directly employed by an insurer to handle its claims, as opposed to a contracted or policyholder-hired adjuster.
detail: A staff adjuster is the insurer's own employee, handling claims from a desk or in the field on salary rather than per assignment. They carry the company's procedures and authority limits, escalating large or disputed files. They contrast with independent adjusters hired per claim and public adjusters hired by policyholders. For routine claims a staff adjuster is the face of the insurer, and their workload and authority shape how quickly and generously everyday claims get settled.

plain: A crash deliberately caused or faked to file injury and damage claims — a classic organized-fraud scheme.
snappy: A collision intentionally engineered or fabricated by fraudsters to generate bogus injury and property-damage claims.
detail: A staged accident is hard fraud on the road: fraudsters deliberately cause a crash — slamming on the brakes to be rear-ended, or waving a victim forward into a collision — then file inflated claims for phantom injuries and damage, often with crooked clinics and lawyers in on it. Rings run them at scale, and the National Insurance Crime Bureau tracks the patterns. They're dangerous as well as costly, since real bystanders can be hurt in a manufactured wreck.

plain: The home state whose regulator leads oversight of an insurer, even as it operates in many states.
snappy: The state where an insurer is incorporated and primarily regulated, leading its solvency oversight nationwide.
detail: An insurer's state of domicile is its regulatory home: the state where it's incorporated, whose department of insurance takes the lead in examining its finances and is the domiciliary regulator other states defer to for solvency. The insurer must also be licensed in every other state where it sells, but the home state runs point. Companies choose domiciles partly for the regulatory climate, which is why so many incorporate in states known for sophisticated, business-friendly insurance departments.

plain: The conservative accounting rules insurers must use for regulators — focused on whether claims can be paid, not on profit.
snappy: The conservative, solvency-focused accounting standards insurers follow in regulatory filings, distinct from standard GAAP.
detail: Statutory accounting is regulation's own ledger: a conservative rulebook insurers use in their filings to the state, designed to answer one question — can this company pay claims? It values assets cautiously, admitting only those readily turned to cash, and recognizes liabilities early. That makes it stricter than the GAAP accounting used for investors, who care about earnings. The gap between the two is why an insurer can look modestly profitable to shareholders yet be measured far more sternly for solvency.

plain: A rule that makes you try a cheaper drug first and fail on it before the plan covers a pricier one.
snappy: A plan policy requiring patients to try lower-cost drugs before a more expensive option is covered.
detail: Under step therapy — "fail first" — your plan won't pay for the costly medication your doctor prefers until you've tried and not responded to cheaper alternatives. It saves money but can delay effective treatment, and patient groups lobby states to limit it. You'll meet it at the pharmacy counter when a prescription is rejected with a note to try the preferred drug first.

plain: An insurer owned by shareholders, run to earn them a profit — the standard corporate form.
snappy: An insurer organized as a stock corporation, owned by shareholders who provide capital and receive its profits.
detail: A stock insurance company is an insurer built like any other public corporation: shareholders own it, supply its capital, and collect its profits through dividends and a rising share price. That access to equity markets makes raising capital easier than for a mutual, but it also brings pressure to deliver returns each quarter. Most large publicly traded insurers take this form. Sometimes a mutual converts to it — demutualization — to tap stock markets, turning its policyholder-owners into shareholders.

plain: Coverage that protects a self-funded employer from huge or unexpectedly high medical claims.
snappy: Insurance reimbursing a self-funded plan once claims pass a set threshold, capping the employer's medical exposure.
detail: An employer paying its own claims could be sunk by one premature baby or transplant. Stop-loss insurance caps that risk: specific stop-loss covers any single person's claims above a deductible, while aggregate stop-loss covers total claims above an expected level. It's reinsurance for self-funded plans in all but name, and it's what makes self-funding safe enough for mid-sized employers to attempt.

plain: Legal responsibility without any need to prove carelessness — the harm and the cause are enough.
snappy: Liability imposed regardless of fault or intent, applied to defective products and abnormally dangerous activities.
detail: Strict liability skips the question of fault: if a defective product injures a user or an abnormally dangerous activity like blasting causes damage, the responsible party pays whether or not it was careful. Courts apply it where the activity or product is risky enough that society puts the cost on whoever profits from it. It dramatically widens products liability exposure, since an injured plaintiff need only prove the defect and the harm, not negligence.

plain: A legal payout paid out as steady installments over years instead of one lump sum, often funded by an annuity.
snappy: An arrangement resolving a claim through scheduled future payments, usually funded by an annuity, often tax-free for injuries.
detail: A structured settlement resolves a lawsuit — typically a personal-injury or wrongful-death claim — by paying the plaintiff over years rather than all at once, with the defendant's insurer buying an annuity to fund the schedule. Payments for physical injury are generally tax-free, and the structure protects claimants from spending a lump sum too fast. A secondary market lets recipients sell future payments for cash, a practice courts must approve.

plain: A smaller cap inside your policy that limits payment for one specific kind of loss.
snappy: A cap below the overall policy limit applying to a particular category of loss, such as jewellery or water damage.
detail: Your homeowners policy might carry a $300,000 limit overall but a $1,500 sublimit on jewellery, so a stolen engagement ring is barely covered. Sublimits hide in the fine print and surprise people at claim time. To restore full value you schedule the item — listing it specifically for an extra premium. Commercial policies use sublimits heavily for floods, earthquakes, and cyber losses.

plain: After paying your claim, the insurer steps into your shoes to chase whoever actually caused the loss.
snappy: The right of the insurer, after paying a claim, to pursue the third party responsible and recover what it paid out.
detail: If another driver totals your car, your insurer may pay you and then subrogate — sue or bill the at-fault driver's insurer to get its money back. Successful subrogation can return your deductible to you. The principle stops the wrongdoer escaping just because you had insurance, and it keeps you from collecting twice. Health insurers subrogate too, clawing back from accident settlements they helped fund.

plain: The money an insurer claws back from the party that caused a loss after it has paid its own policyholder.
snappy: The amount an insurer recovers from a liable third party to offset a claim it has already paid to its insured.
detail: After paying a claim, an insurer often chases the wrongdoer who caused it — that pursuit is subrogation, and what it collects is the subrogation recovery. A health insurer recovers from the at-fault driver's auto insurer; a property insurer recovers from the contractor who started the fire. Recoveries reduce the net cost of claims and can refund the policyholder's deductible. The made whole doctrine governs who gets paid first when the recovery isn't enough to cover everyone.

plain: An applicant whose health makes them riskier than average, so they pay a higher life insurance premium.
snappy: An applicant rated worse than standard for health or lifestyle, charged an extra premium or table rating, or declined.
detail: When underwriting finds elevated risk — a serious illness, dangerous hobby, or poor history — the applicant is classed substandard, or "rated," and pays a surcharge expressed as a table rating, each table adding a set percentage to the standard premium. It's the insurer's way of covering rather than refusing higher-risk lives. Improve your health and some insurers will reconsider the rating later.

plain: A life policy provision that limits the payout if the insured dies by suicide in the first couple of years.
snappy: A clause excluding suicide deaths within an initial period, usually two years, refunding premiums instead of paying.
detail: Most life policies contain a suicide clause: if the insured dies by suicide within the first two years, the insurer returns the premiums paid rather than the death benefit. After that window, suicide is generally covered like any other death. The provision, paralleling the contestability period, exists to deter buying coverage with that intent while not punishing families years later.

plain: An extra charge added to your premium after an at-fault accident or violation.
snappy: A premium increase an insurer applies after an at-fault accident, ticket, or other risk event, often lasting several years.
detail: A surcharge is the penalty baked into your next premium after an at-fault accident, speeding ticket, or DUI — typically lasting three to five years before it rolls off. It's why one bad year can cost far more than the claim itself. Accident-forgiveness features waive the first surcharge for loyal drivers. Comparing how aggressively insurers surcharge, not just their base rates, matters for drivers with a blemish.

plain: A three-party guarantee that a job will get done — the insurer pays if the contractor fails to deliver.
snappy: A guarantee in which a surety promises a project owner that a contractor will fulfil an obligation, backing it financially if not.
detail: A surety bond isn't quite insurance — it's a three-party promise. The surety guarantees to the owner (the obligee) that the contractor (the principal) will perform the work, and pays out if the contractor defaults. Unlike insurance, the surety expects to be repaid by the contractor after a claim, so it underwrites like a lender. Construction bid, performance, and payment bonds are the classic forms, often required before a contractor can take on public work.

plain: The market for coverage the standard insurers won't write — flexible, specialized, and lightly regulated.
snappy: Coverage placed with non-admitted insurers for risks the admitted market declines, exempt from rate and form regulation.
detail: Surplus lines, also called excess and surplus or E&S, is the safety valve of the insurance market: when admitted carriers decline a risk — a nightclub, a vacant building, a novel cyber exposure — it can be placed with a non-admitted surplus lines insurer free to set its own terms and price. A licensed surplus lines broker must confirm the admitted market truly turned it down, collect a special premium tax, and warn the buyer there's no guaranty fund. The market grows whenever standard insurers retreat from a risk.

plain: A specially licensed broker who places coverage with non-admitted insurers when the standard market says no.
snappy: A broker licensed to place business with surplus lines insurers after confirming the admitted market has declined the risk.
detail: A surplus lines broker is the gatekeeper to the non-admitted market: holding a special licence, they may place a risk with a surplus lines insurer only after documenting that licensed admitted carriers wouldn't take it — the diligent-search requirement. They also collect and remit the surplus lines premium tax and disclose to the buyer that no guaranty fund stands behind the policy. Retail agents who lack the licence route hard-to-place accounts through them, often via a wholesale broker.

plain: An insurer that covers hard-to-place risks without a state licence — more flexible, but not guaranty-fund protected.
snappy: An insurer not licensed in a state that may still cover risks the admitted market declines, free of rate and form approval.
detail: A surplus lines, or non-admitted, insurer writes the risks standard carriers won't: a coastal property, a risky startup, an unusual liability. It isn't licensed in the state and so escapes rate and form regulation, gaining the freedom to price and craft coverage as the risk demands. The catch for buyers is no guaranty association backstop if it fails, so states require these insurers to be financially vetted and the coverage placed through a licensed surplus lines broker.

plain: A proportional treaty that reinsures only the part of each policy above the insurer's chosen retention line.
snappy: A proportional treaty ceding the portion of each risk that exceeds the cedent's retention, leaving small risks fully retained.
detail: Surplus share is proportional reinsurance with a twist: instead of a flat percentage of everything, the cedent keeps a set retention on each risk and cedes only the surplus above it, so the reinsured share varies policy by policy. Small risks stay entirely with the insurer; large ones are heavily ceded. It lets a carrier keep all the premium on routine business while still writing policies far larger than its retention. The treaty's capacity is measured in lines — multiples of the retention.

plain: A penalty the insurer keeps if you cash out a life policy or annuity in its early years.
snappy: A fee deducted when a policyholder surrenders or over-withdraws from permanent life or an annuity, declining over time.
detail: Surrender charges let insurers recover the upfront costs of writing a policy if you bail out early. On annuities and permanent life they typically start high — say 7% — and step down to zero over several years. They're why these products are sold as long-term commitments and why surrendering in year two stings. Free-withdrawal provisions let you take a small slice each year without the charge.

plain: The years after buying an annuity when cashing out early costs you a penalty.
snappy: The span, often six to ten years, during which surrendering an annuity beyond the free amount incurs a declining charge.
detail: The surrender period is the lock-up on an annuity: cash out, or withdraw beyond the free amount, during these years and a surrender charge applies, usually starting high and stepping down to zero. It lets the insurer recoup upfront costs and commissions. Buyers must be sure they won't need the money during this window — surrendering a long-surrender-period annuity early is one of the costliest mistakes in personal finance.

plain: One policy on two people that pays only after both have died — popular for passing wealth to heirs.
snappy: Permanent life insurance covering two lives and paying the death benefit only on the second death, used in estate planning.
detail: Survivorship life — second-to-die — insures a couple under one policy and pays out when the second spouse dies, which is when estate taxes typically come due. Because two lives must end before it pays, the premium is lower than two separate policies. Estate planners pair it with an irrevocable life insurance trust to give heirs cash to pay estate tax without selling the family business or property.

plain: An extension that lets you report old claims after a claims-made policy ends.
snappy: An extended reporting period on a claims-made policy that covers claims filed after expiration for prior covered acts.
detail: When a doctor retires or switches insurers, tail coverage keeps the old claims-made policy responsive to lawsuits that surface later over past treatment. Without it, every patient encounter becomes uninsured the day the policy lapses. The tail can be costly — often a multiple of the annual premium — but for long-tail professions it's the difference between a clean exit and lingering personal exposure.

plain: The small chance of an extreme loss far worse than the typical year — the dangerous edge of the distribution.
snappy: The risk of rare, severe outcomes in the far tail of a loss distribution, beyond what normal years suggest.
detail: Tail risk lives at the far end of the bell curve, where outcomes are unlikely but devastating: the once-in-a-century quake, the simultaneous failure of many bets thought independent. Insurers and actuaries model it because pricing off average years badly understates what a bad tail can cost. Capital requirements, catastrophe reinsurance, and stress tests all exist to make sure a company survives a tail event, not just an ordinary one. Underestimating the tail is how insurers fail.

plain: Putting off paying tax on investment growth until you actually withdraw the money.
snappy: Postponing tax on earnings until withdrawal, letting gains compound untaxed — a core selling point of annuities and cash value.
detail: Tax deferral lets money grow without the yearly drag of taxes, so gains compound on themselves until you take them out — the headline benefit of annuities, permanent life cash value, and retirement accounts. The catch is that deferred gains are eventually taxed, often as ordinary income, and early withdrawals before age 59½ can trigger a penalty. Whether deferral beats a taxable account depends on fees, time, and your future tax bracket.

plain: The cheapest life insurance — it covers you for a set number of years and pays only if you die during them.
snappy: Life insurance covering a fixed term that pays a death benefit only if the insured dies within it, with no cash value.
detail: Term life is the no-frills option: pick a length — 10, 20, or 30 years — and a face amount, and the policy pays the death benefit if you die inside the term. Premiums are low because most policies never pay out; outlive the term and coverage simply ends. It's the practical choice for covering a mortgage or raising children, when you need a big death benefit for the lowest premium.

plain: Coverage for property and liability losses from a terrorist attack, backstopped by a federal program.
snappy: Coverage for losses caused by certified acts of terrorism, supported by a federal reinsurance backstop for large attacks.
detail: After September 11, insurers fled the terrorism risk and a federal backstop was created so coverage could survive: the government shares the cost of losses from a certified attack above a high threshold, letting private insurers keep offering it. Commercial property and liability policies must now offer terrorism coverage, which businesses can accept or decline. Lenders often require it on large properties, so the backstop quietly underpins much commercial real-estate finance.

plain: A firm hired to process claims for a self-insured employer or insurer that doesn't handle them in-house.
snappy: An outside organization that handles claims administration, and sometimes other functions, on behalf of an insurer or self-insured plan.
detail: A third-party administrator runs claims for someone else: a self-insured employer's health or workers' comp claims, or an insurer's overflow. The administrator processes first notice of loss, adjusts, and pays, while the financial risk stays with the plan or insurer behind it. Self-insurance leans on them heavily, since an employer funding its own losses still needs professional claim handling. They're the reason a worker's claim can look identical whether a carrier or a self-insured plan ultimately foots the bill.

plain: Insurance that pays other people for harm you caused them.
snappy: Liability coverage that pays outsiders the insured is legally responsible for injuring or whose property they damaged.
detail: When you rear-end another driver, your liability coverage is third-party — it pays the other driver, not you. The injured outsider is the third party (you and the insurer are the first two). These policies also pay to defend you against the resulting lawsuit. The insurer's duty to a third-party claimant is fair dealing, a notch below the good faith it owes its own insured.

plain: A one-time policy protecting a home buyer or lender against hidden ownership problems from the property's past.
snappy: Coverage protecting against losses from defects in a property's title — liens, errors, fraud — predating the purchase.
detail: Unlike most insurance, title insurance looks backward: it protects against problems already lurking in a property's ownership history — an unpaid lien, a forged deed, a missed heir, a clerical error — that could surface after you buy. Bought once at closing with a single premium, it comes in two forms: lender's title insurance protecting the bank, and owner's title insurance protecting your equity. It's standard in nearly every US home purchase.

plain: The traditional approach where the at-fault driver's insurer pays everyone they harmed.
snappy: An auto regime where the driver at fault, through their liability coverage, is responsible for others' injury and damage.
detail: In a tort state — the system in most of the US — the driver who caused the crash is liable, and their bodily injury and property damage liability coverage pays the victims, who can also sue for pain and suffering. It contrasts with no-fault, where each driver's own policy pays first. The tort system makes establishing fault central to every claim, which is why adjusters and police reports matter so much.

plain: When repairing a damaged car would cost more than it's worth, so the insurer pays its value instead.
snappy: A vehicle whose repair cost (plus salvage) exceeds its actual cash value or a state threshold, settled by paying its value.
detail: A car is a total loss — "totaled" — when repairs would cost more than the vehicle is worth or exceed a state total-loss threshold. Rather than fix it, the insurer pays the actual cash value, takes the wreck for salvage, and you settle any loan, where gap insurance can cover a shortfall. Disputes usually centre on the actual cash value the insurer assigns, which owners often argue is too low.

plain: The point — set by state or insurer — where damage is bad enough to declare a car a total loss.
snappy: The percentage of a vehicle's value at which damage triggers a total-loss settlement instead of repair.
detail: States and insurers set a total loss threshold — often 70% to 80% of the car's value, or a formula comparing repair plus salvage to value — that decides when a damaged car is written off rather than fixed. Cross it and the insurer pays actual cash value and takes the salvage. The threshold explains why two similar dents can end differently: one repairs, the other totals, depending on the car's value.

plain: Coverage that pays a supplier when a business customer fails to pay its invoices.
snappy: Coverage protecting sellers against the risk that commercial customers default on payment for goods or services delivered.
detail: Trade credit insurance protects a company's receivables: if a customer goes bankrupt or simply doesn't pay, the insurer covers most of the unpaid invoice. Exporters and manufacturers selling on terms use it to safely extend credit, enter new markets, and borrow against insured receivables at better rates. It shifts a core business risk — that the buyer won't pay — onto an insurer that monitors the creditworthiness of the company's customers.

plain: A standing deal where a reinsurer automatically takes an agreed slice of a whole class of the insurer's policies.
snappy: A reinsurance agreement covering a defined book of business automatically, without underwriting each risk individually.
detail: Treaty reinsurance is the wholesale arrangement: one contract under which the reinsurer agrees to accept an agreed share of every policy in a defined book — all the cedent's homeowners business, say — automatically, no risk-by-risk review. It gives the primary insurer reliable, ongoing capacity and the reinsurer a diversified slice of a whole portfolio. It contrasts with facultative reinsurance, which is negotiated one risk at a time for the unusual or oversized exposures a treaty doesn't neatly cover.

plain: An adjustment that ages old loss data forward to today's cost level, accounting for inflation and changing behaviour.
snappy: A multiplier applied in ratemaking to project historical losses to the cost levels expected during the future policy period.
detail: Historical losses are stale by the time they're used to set tomorrow's rates, so actuaries apply trend factors to age them forward: medical and repair inflation, rising jury awards, and shifts in how often people claim all push future costs above the past. Frequency and severity are usually trended separately. Choosing the trend is one of ratemaking's most consequential judgments — too low and the rate is inadequate before it even takes effect, too high and it overshoots the market.

plain: Talking a customer into dropping one policy for another using misleading comparisons — usually to earn a fresh commission.
snappy: Inducing a policyholder to replace a policy through misrepresentation, often to the customer's detriment and the agent's gain.
detail: Twisting is replacement by deception: an agent persuades a customer to surrender an existing policy and buy a new one using misleading or incomplete comparisons, typically to pocket a new commission. The switch often harms the customer — a fresh contestability period on life insurance, surrender charges, lost benefits. It's a named unfair trade practice that regulators punish, distinct from churning, where the agent does the same thing using policies from the same insurer rather than luring the customer to a competitor.

plain: The final, all-in cost of a loss to the reinsured after every recovery and expense is counted — the figure reinsurance pays on.
snappy: The total loss retained by the cedent after deductions like salvage and other reinsurance, plus loss adjustment expense, on which a layer responds.
detail: Ultimate net loss is the number a reinsurance layer actually measures against its attachment point: the cedent's loss once salvage, subrogation, and any inuring reinsurance are subtracted and loss adjustment expense is added in. Defining it precisely matters, because whether costs like defence count toward the loss can decide whether a layer is breached. Disputes over what belongs in the ultimate net loss are among the most common in reinsurance claims.

plain: Extra liability coverage that sits on top of your home and auto policies for catastrophic claims.
snappy: A policy adding a layer of liability limit above auto, home, or business coverage, plus some broader protection.
detail: When a lawsuit blows past your auto or homeowners liability limit, an umbrella policy picks up the next million or more — cheap protection for high-net-worth families and landlords. It also fills some gaps the underlying policies exclude. Umbrellas require you to carry minimum underlying limits first, then attach above them. The name fits: one policy spreads over several others to catch the rare, ruinous claim.

plain: A neutral third party who breaks the tie when a policyholder's and insurer's appraisers disagree on a loss's value.
snappy: An impartial party who resolves a valuation dispute under the appraisal clause when the two sides' appraisers cannot agree.
detail: When a policyholder and insurer invoke the appraisal clause to settle a dispute over how much a loss is worth, each picks an appraiser, and if the two can't agree they turn to an umpire. The umpire is a neutral expert whose decision, joined by either appraiser, sets the binding amount. It's a faster, cheaper alternative to a lawsuit for pure valuation fights — though it resolves the number, not whether the loss was covered in the first place.

plain: Coverage that fills the gap when an at-fault driver's insurance is too small to cover your injuries.
snappy: Coverage paying the insured when an at-fault driver's liability limits are too low to cover the full injury claim.
detail: When the driver who hurt you carries only minimum liability coverage and your injuries cost far more, underinsured motorist coverage pays the difference up to your own limit. It pairs with uninsured motorist coverage, the two often bundled together. Given how low many state-minimum limits are, it's one of the most valuable and overlooked auto coverages, protecting you from other people's thin policies.

plain: The person or system that decides whether an insurer takes on a risk and what to charge for it.
snappy: An insurance professional who evaluates risks, sets terms and pricing, and decides whether to accept or decline applications.
detail: An underwriter is the insurer's risk decision-maker, weighing each application against the company's underwriting guidelines and risk appetite. They accept clean risks at standard rates, load or exclude the marginal ones, and decline what falls outside appetite. In personal lines much of this is now automated, while complex commercial and life risks still pass under a human underwriter's eye. The title traces to marine insurers who literally signed their names under a risk at Lloyd's.

plain: The insurer's decision of whether to cover you and at what price, based on how risky you look.
snappy: The process of evaluating an applicant's risk to decide whether to offer coverage, on what terms, and at what premium.
detail: Underwriting is the gatekeeping at the heart of insurance: examining an application, its risk factors, and its loss history to decide whether to accept the risk, exclude part of it, or decline, and what premium fairly matches it. Do it too loosely and claims swamp the pool; too strictly and there's nothing to sell. Medical exams, motor vehicle reports, credit-based insurance scores, and increasingly automated models all feed the call.

plain: The boom-and-bust rhythm of insurance pricing, swinging between cheap, easy coverage and expensive, scarce coverage.
snappy: The recurring swing of insurance markets between soft conditions of low prices and ample capacity and hard conditions of high prices and scarcity.
detail: The underwriting cycle is the tide insurance pricing runs on: in a soft market, ample capital and competition push premiums down and coverage is easy to get; losses and shrinking capital then flip it to a hard market of rising premiums, tighter terms, and scarce capacity. Big catastrophes, investment swings, and reinsurance pricing all drive the turns. Buyers feel it as years when insurance is cheap and plentiful giving way, sometimes abruptly, to years when it's dear and hard to find.

plain: The insurer's internal rulebook telling underwriters which risks to accept, price up, or refuse.
snappy: An insurer's internal standards specifying acceptable risks, required information, pricing tiers, and grounds for declination.
detail: Underwriting guidelines are the playbook that keeps an insurer's risk-taking consistent: which risks are preferred, which need extra information, which carry surcharges or exclusions, and which to decline outright. They translate the company's risk appetite into day-to-day decisions and into the automated rules that price online quotes. Filed portions are visible to regulators checking for unfair discrimination; the rest is closely guarded, since they encode how an insurer believes it can win.

plain: The money an insurer makes from insurance itself — premiums minus claims and expenses — before investment income.
snappy: The profit from core insurance operations: earned premium less incurred losses and expenses, excluding investment returns.
detail: Underwriting profit isolates how well an insurer does at its actual job: collecting premium and paying out fewer claims and expenses than it took in. It equals earned premium minus losses and expenses, and a combined ratio under 100% is the same thing said as a percentage. Many insurers run a small underwriting loss and make their money investing the float in the meantime, but a durable underwriting profit is the mark of genuinely good pricing and risk selection.

plain: The part of premium you've paid for coverage that hasn't happened yet — refundable if you cancel early.
snappy: The prepaid premium covering the remaining policy period, held as a liability and refundable on cancellation.
detail: If you cancel a six-month auto policy after two months, the four months of unearned premium come back to you, minus any short-rate penalty. Insurers must hold unearned premium as a reserve — a liability on the balance sheet — because they still owe that coverage. Regulators watch the unearned premium reserve to be sure a carrier can deliver the protection it has already been paid for.

plain: The specific claim-handling abuses — stalling, lowballing, ignoring you — that state law bans insurers from committing.
snappy: A statutory list of prohibited insurer claim behaviors, such as unreasonable delay, inadequate investigation, or lowball offers.
detail: Most states have adopted an Unfair Claims Settlement Practices Act that spells out what insurers may not do: misrepresent policy terms, drag out an investigation, force claimants to sue to get a fair amount, or deny without a reasonable basis. Regulators enforce it through fines and market-conduct exams, and a pattern of violations is powerful evidence in a bad-faith suit. It's the rulebook that turns the vague promise of fair dealing into specific, punishable claim-handling standards.

plain: The deceptive sales and marketing tactics state law specifically bans insurers and agents from using.
snappy: A statutory category of prohibited insurer and producer conduct, including misrepresentation, false advertising, and improper inducements.
detail: Most states have an Unfair Trade Practices Act listing the marketing and sales conduct insurers and agents may not engage in: misrepresenting policies, false or misleading advertising, unfair discrimination, and improper inducements like rebating. It's the sales-side companion to the rules against unfair claims settlement practices, and regulators enforce it through market conduct exams, fines, and licence actions. Specific abuses like twisting and churning are named violations under it, giving regulators clear grounds to punish predatory selling.

plain: Coverage that pays you when an at-fault driver has no insurance to cover your injuries.
snappy: Coverage paying the insured for injuries (and sometimes damage) caused by an at-fault driver who carries no insurance.
detail: Roughly one in eight US drivers is uninsured, so uninsured motorist coverage steps in when the at-fault driver has no policy — paying your medical bills and lost wages as their liability coverage would have. It also typically covers hit-and-run crashes where the other driver flees. Many states require it. It's cheap relative to the protection it provides, filling the hole left by drivers who ignore the law.

plain: Flexible permanent life insurance that lets you adjust your premiums and death benefit over time.
snappy: Permanent life insurance with adjustable premiums and death benefit, where cash value earns interest set by the insurer.
detail: Universal life unbundles whole life into flexible parts: within limits you can raise or lower the premium and the death benefit, and the cash value earns a credited interest rate the insurer declares. That flexibility cuts both ways — underfund it for years and rising internal costs can drain the cash value and lapse the policy, a problem that has produced lawsuits and surprise premium calls for older policyholders.

plain: Car insurance that prices your premium on how you actually drive, tracked by an app or device.
snappy: Auto coverage that sets premiums from telematics data on mileage, braking, speed, and time of day rather than proxies alone.
detail: Usage-based insurance uses a plug-in device or phone app to track how, when, and how far you drive — hard braking, speeding, late-night trips, total mileage — and prices the premium accordingly. Safe drivers can save; aggressive ones may pay more or lose the discount. Marketed as fairer than traditional rating, it raises privacy questions about who sees your driving data and how long it's kept.

plain: The plan's process of checking whether the care you're getting is necessary and covered.
snappy: A managed-care process evaluating the medical necessity and appropriateness of services before, during, or after care.
